stem: 7 years old girl presented with breast development and pubic hair , breast tanner 3 and pubic hair tanner 2 , normal fsh , lh , brain mri normal , high estradiol ?
why_right: A 7-year-old with breast Tanner 3 and pubic hair, high estradiol but gonadotropins that are not raised ("normal FSH, LH") and a "normal" brain MRI indicates estrogen production independent of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis: peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) precocious puberty, e.g. ovarian cyst or tumor, McCune-Albright, exogenous estrogen.
why_wrong_block: A. Central precocious puberty is driven by early activation of the HPG axis, so LH and FSH are raised into the pubertal range (especially after GnRH stimulation); non-raised gonadotropins with high estradiol argue against it.
key_concept:
Precocious puberty in girls: signs before age 8.
  • Central: high LH/FSH (stimulated LH rise), mostly idiopathic in girls; MRI brain; treat with GnRH agonist
  • Peripheral: high sex steroid with low/normal (suppressed) LH/FSH
  • Peripheral causes: ovarian cyst/tumor, McCune-Albright, adrenal, exogenous estrogen
  • Next step for peripheral: pelvic ultrasound
exam_pearl: High estradiol with gonadotropins that fail to rise = peripheral; read the LH/FSH, not the Tanner stage.

stem: Child 2 moth features (I forget ) protruded tongue , on cardiac exam significant murmur?
key_concept:
Syndrome first, then its signature heart lesion.
  • Down syndrome: AVSD (atrioventricular canal) most characteristic; VSD and ASD also occur
  • Turner syndrome: coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve
  • Congenital rubella: PDA
  • Williams syndrome: supravalvular aortic stenosis
  • Noonan syndrome: pulmonary valve stenosis
  • AVSD clue: superior QRS axis on ECG
exam_pearl: If the stem gives Down features, the answer is AVSD; VSD wins only when the question asks for the most common CHD in general.

stem: Uncontrolled BA + greasy foul smell stool , next investigation?
why_right: Uncontrolled asthma together with greasy, foul smelling stool (steatorrhea) is cystic fibrosis until proven otherwise: chronic airway disease plus pancreatic insufficiency. The lead-in asks for the next investigation, and the first diagnostic test for suspected CF is the sweat chloride test. CFTR genetic testing confirms or is used when sweat results are borderline.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ct chest: shows bronchiectasis or structural lung damage once CF is known, but it cannot diagnose CF and does not explain the steatorrhea.
B. Brocho lavage: used to obtain airway cultures (for example Pseudomonas) or to evaluate infection in established lung disease; it is invasive and not a diagnostic test for CF.
key_concept:
Respiratory symptoms + malabsorption in a child = cystic fibrosis; first test is sweat chloride.
  • Diagnosis needs one clinical or context criterion plus one laboratory criterion
  • Lab criteria: raised sweat chloride on two occasions, or two CF-causing CFTR mutations
  • Other clues: failure to thrive, rectal prolapse, nasal polyps, meconium ileus
  • Sibling of an affected child: CFTR genetic testing
exam_pearl: Asthma that will not settle plus steatorrhea is not just bad asthma: think CF and order a sweat test.

stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with short stature, primary amenorrhea, and absent secondary sexual characteristics. Her karyotype is 45,X. What is the most appropriate treatment at this time?
why_right: The 45,X karyotype with short stature and absent puberty is Turner syndrome, where short stature is caused by SHOX haploinsufficiency, not GH deficiency. This recall's key is growth hormone because the classic teaching is to maximise height first while the epiphyses are open, since estrogen accelerates epiphyseal fusion and ends growth. Estrogen is then added to induce puberty.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral contraceptive pills: not used to start puberty; induction uses low-dose estrogen increased gradually, and combined pills come later only for maintenance.
C. Estrogen therapy: needed in Turner syndrome to induce breasts and menses, so it is part of her care; the key ranks it after GH because early full-dose estrogen closes the growth plates and limits final height.
D. Gonadotropin replacement therapy: useless here because the problem is primary ovarian failure (streak gonads) with high FSH and LH; gonadotropins are for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
key_concept:
Turner syndrome treatment: height first, then puberty.
  • Diagnosis: karyotype 45,X (mosaicism possible)
  • Short stature: GH therapy while epiphyses are open
  • Ovarian failure: low-dose estrogen to induce puberty, progestin added later for cycles
  • Gonadotropins are not useful: FSH and LH are already high
  • Screen heart (coarctation, bicuspid valve) and kidneys (horseshoe kidney)
exam_pearl: In Turner syndrome the ovaries, not the pituitary, have failed: never give gonadotropins.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2517).

stem: Child(I think 2 month) came with his mother concern about chicken Pox infection after his exposure with child with chicken Pox several days. Child now asymptomatic what to do
why_right: A healthy 2-month-old exposed to chickenpox who is now asymptomatic needs no specific intervention, so the answer is to reassure the mother. Varicella immunoglobulin is reserved for high-risk exposures such as immunocompromised children, pregnant women, newborns whose mother develops varicella around delivery, and hospitalised preterm infants. The vaccine cannot be given before 12 months, and antibiotics have no role against a virus.
why_wrong_block:
B. give VZIG: right for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised child, newborn whose mother has varicella from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, preterm infants in hospital); a healthy term 2-month-old is not in these groups.
C. give chicken box vaccine: live varicella vaccine is not licensed under 12 months, so it cannot be used for post-exposure prophylaxis in a 2-month-old.
D. give prophylaxis antibiotics: varicella is viral; antibiotics are only for secondary bacterial skin infection of established lesions.
key_concept:
Varicella post-exposure: decide by host risk and age.
  • Healthy infant under 12 months, asymptomatic: reassure and observe
  • Healthy non-immune child 12 months or older: vaccine within 3 to 5 days
  • Immunocompromised, pregnant, at-risk newborn or preterm: VZIG (IVIG if VZIG unavailable)
  • Antibiotics: never as prophylaxis
exam_pearl: Age decides it: under 12 months the vaccine is not an option, and a healthy term infant does not qualify for VZIG.

stem: 6 years came with his mother concern about chichen box infection after his exposure with child with chicken box 2 days. Child now asymptomatic what to do?
why_right: A healthy 6-year-old exposed to chickenpox 2 days ago who is asymptomatic is within the post-exposure window, so varicella vaccine is the answer (assuming he is not already immune). Given within 3 days, and up to 5 days, of exposure it can prevent or modify the illness, and it also protects against future exposures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observe for a few days: lets the post-exposure window close; observation alone fits a healthy infant too young for the vaccine, not a 6-year-old who can be vaccinated.
B. give IVIG: passive immunisation is for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised, pregnant, at-risk newborns) when VZIG is unavailable; a healthy child gets the vaccine instead.
D. I don't remember but irrelevant: a placeholder from the recall, not a management option.
key_concept:
Healthy non-immune child 12 months or older exposed to varicella: vaccinate within 3 to 5 days.
  • Vaccine within 3 days is most effective, up to 5 days acceptable
  • Immunocompromised or pregnant: VZIG, not live vaccine
  • Under 12 months and healthy: reassure
  • Already immune (prior disease or two doses): nothing needed
exam_pearl: Timing flips it: exposure within 5 days in a healthy child over 12 months = vaccine; a high-risk host = immunoglobulin.

stem: A post-operative patient who underwent a subtotal colectomy has a nasogastric tube set to high-level continuous suction. Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum potassium level of 2.8 mmol/L (low). What is the primary cause of this patient's hypokalemia?
OptC: Renal potassium wasting due to aldosterone
highlight_terms_source: nasogastric tube set to high-level continuous suction
why_right: The decisive clue is the nasogastric tube on high continuous suction after a subtotal colectomy. Removal of gastric fluid causes direct potassium loss and, more importantly, loss of HCl leading to metabolic alkalosis and volume depletion, which drives further renal potassium loss. The root cause of the hypokalemia is therefore the NG suction.
why_wrong_block:
B. Inadequate dietary intake: being nil by mouth contributes little over a short postoperative period because the kidney conserves potassium; it is a cause in prolonged starvation or malnutrition.
C. Renal potassium wasting due to aldosterone: this is the mechanism through which NG suction lowers potassium (volume loss and alkalosis activate aldosterone), but it is secondary; primary aldosteronism would show hypertension with no GI loss.
D. Intraoperative fluid shift: transcellular shifts (insulin, beta agonists, alkalosis) are transient and would not explain persistent hypokalemia during ongoing high-volume suction.
key_concept:
Hypokalemia from upper GI loss (vomiting or NG suction):
  • Lose HCl: metabolic alkalosis
  • Lose volume: secondary hyperaldosteronism
  • Result: hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with renal K wasting
  • Treat: replace volume with saline plus KCl
  • Hypokalemia can prolong postoperative ileus
exam_pearl: When a cause (NG suction) and its mechanism (aldosterone driven renal loss) are both options, "primary cause" asks for the cause.

stem: Psyco insomnia hx depressive family hx of mania presents with symptoms of insomnia and maybe irritability?
key_concept:
Insomnia in a patient with a mood history: decide which sleep problem it is.
  • Cannot sleep, tired next day, no mood episode: sleep hygiene / CBT-I
  • Low mood + anhedonia + insomnia ≥2 weeks: depression, treat after bipolar screen
  • Little sleep but full of energy, irritable: hypomania/mania, mood stabilizer
  • Family history of mania: avoid antidepressant monotherapy
exam_pearl: Decreased NEED for sleep with high energy is mania; insomnia with fatigue is not.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 4-day-old infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for episodes of apnea. On examination, a continuous machinery-like murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border, and a wide pulse pressure is noted. A chest X-ray reveals bilateral pulmonary congestion ("wet lung"). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptC: Urgent surgical ligation of the ductus
why_right: A continuous machinery murmur at the left upper sternal border with a wide pulse pressure is a patent ductus arteriosus. In a 4-day-old in the NICU with apnea and pulmonary congestion, the ductus is hemodynamically significant, so the next step is pharmacological closure with a prostaglandin inhibitor (indomethacin or ibuprofen) to constrict the duct.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluid restriction and diuretics: supportive measures that may accompany treatment, but they do not close the ductus and so do not address the cause of the congestion.
C. Urgent surgical ligation of the ductus: reserved for a significant PDA that fails medical closure or when NSAIDs are contraindicated (for example renal failure, active bleeding, NEC).
D. Prostaglandin E1 infusion: keeps the ductus OPEN; it is right for duct-dependent lesions such as TGA or critical coarctation, and here it would worsen the shunt.
key_concept:
Ductus drugs work in opposite directions.
  • Close a significant PDA: NSAID (indomethacin or ibuprofen); paracetamol is an alternative
  • NSAID fails or contraindicated: surgical ligation or catheter closure
  • Keep duct open in duct-dependent CHD: prostaglandin E1
  • PDA signs: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure
  • Congenital rubella: PDA
exam_pearl: Prostaglandin inhibitor closes the duct; prostaglandin E1 keeps it open: read the option wording carefully.

stem: A newborn infant weighing 2 kg (small for gestational age) is noted to have a depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, upward slanting palpebral fissures, and an elevated epicanthal fold. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: This recall's key is congenital infection screening (TORCH), presumably because the baby is small for gestational age (2 kg) and congenital infection is a recognised cause of growth restriction in a newborn. However, the face described (depressed nasal bridge, upward slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds) is the classic dysmorphism of Down syndrome, which is itself associated with low birth weight. The same question elsewhere in this file is keyed to chromosomal analysis, so treat this key as disputed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chromosomal analysis: the karyotype confirms a suspected chromosomal syndrome such as trisomy 21; it is the keyed answer for the duplicate of this question, but not for this recall.
B. Metabolic screening: routine newborn screening for inborn errors and congenital hypothyroidism; it is not targeted at a dysmorphic face or growth restriction.
D. Skeletal survey: right when skeletal dysplasia (short limbs, abnormal bones) or non-accidental injury is suspected; facial dysmorphism alone does not call for it.
key_concept:
Dysmorphic newborn: name the pattern, then pick the targeted test.
  • Upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds, flat nasal bridge: Down syndrome, confirm by karyotype
  • SGA with microcephaly, cataract, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, calcifications: TORCH screen
  • Short limbs or fractures: skeletal survey
  • Lethargy, poor feeding, jaundice: metabolic or thyroid screen
exam_pearl: SGA alone points to TORCH only when infection signs are present; a Down face points to karyotype.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-2390 → A. Chromosomal analysis. Confirm before the exam.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a firm, partially movable right breast mass that has been present for 3 months. Physical examination and imaging reveal an ill-defined lobulated hypoechoic mass measuring 2 × 2 cm, which is coded as BI-RADS IV. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: An ill-defined, lobulated hypoechoic mass coded BI-RADS IV is suspicious for malignancy. BI-RADS 4 and 5 require a tissue diagnosis, and the test of choice is needle core biopsy (image guided), which gives histology, separates invasive from in situ disease, and allows receptor testing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fine needle aspiration cytology: gives cells only, cannot distinguish invasive from in situ cancer and has a higher non-diagnostic rate; useful for aspirating cysts or sampling axillary nodes.
C. Excisional biopsy: right when core biopsy is non-diagnostic or discordant with imaging, or for lesions such as suspected phyllodes; not the first tissue test.
D. Short-interval follow-up imaging: the plan for BI-RADS 3 (probably benign). Using it for BI-RADS 4 would delay a possible cancer diagnosis.
key_concept:
BI-RADS to action:
  • 0: additional imaging
  • 1 and 2: routine screening
  • 3: short-interval follow-up imaging
  • 4 and 5: core needle biopsy
  • 6: proven malignancy, treat
exam_pearl: Even when imaging looks obviously malignant (BI-RADS 5), the next step is still core biopsy, not surgery.

stem: A 37-week gestation baby on delivery has a heart rate below 100 beats per minute, blue extremities, a weak cry with grimace, and little flexion. What is the most accurate APGAR score?
why_right: Score each sign: heart rate below 100 = 1, blue extremities (pink body, acrocyanosis) = 1, grimace on stimulation = 1, weak cry (weak or irregular respiration) = 1, little flexion = 1. Every component scores 1, so the total is 5.
why_wrong_block:
A. 4: would require one component to score 0 (for example no heart rate, apnea or a limp baby); none is absent here.
C. 7: would need two components at the maximum of 2 (for example heart rate above 100 or a vigorous cry); every sign here is only partial.
D. 9: describes a nearly normal vigorous newborn with only acrocyanosis; this baby is bradycardic, weak and poorly flexed.
key_concept:
APGAR: 5 signs, each 0, 1 or 2.
  • Appearance: blue or pale 0, blue extremities 1, completely pink 2
  • Pulse: absent 0, below 100 = 1, 100 or more = 2
  • Grimace: no response 0, grimace 1, cry or active withdrawal 2
  • Activity: limp 0, some flexion 1, active movement 2
  • Respiration: absent 0, slow, irregular or weak cry 1, good strong cry 2
exam_pearl: Blue extremities score 1, not 0; only a fully blue or pale baby scores 0 for appearance.

stem: A 28-year-old woman underwent surgical excision of a breast mass that was clinically and radiologically suspected to be a fibroadenoma. The final histopathology report reveals a benign fibroadenoma with an incidental finding of a single focus of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) with free surgical margins. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: incidental finding of a single focus of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)
why_right: Classic LCIS found incidentally with a benign fibroadenoma is a risk marker, not a cancer that needs local or systemic treatment. It raises the lifetime risk of invasive cancer in both breasts, so the right step is high-risk screening and follow-up (with discussion of risk-reducing endocrine therapy). The excision is already done and margins are free, so nothing more is needed at the operative site.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simple mastectomy treats large phyllodes tumors or selected cancers; removing one breast for a bilateral risk marker makes no sense. Bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy is only a patient choice in very high-risk women (e.g. BRCA carriers).
B. Adjuvant radiotherapy follows breast-conserving surgery for DCIS or invasive cancer; classic LCIS is not irradiated.
C. Adjuvant chemotherapy is for invasive cancer with systemic risk; LCIS is non-invasive and has no metastatic potential.
key_concept:
Classic LCIS = marker of bilateral risk (a non-obligate precursor), not a lesion that needs clear margins or further local treatment.
  • Classic LCIS incidental on excision: surveillance (clinical exam + imaging) ± chemoprevention
  • Classic LCIS on core biopsy: excision is considered to rule out an associated lesion
  • Pleomorphic or florid LCIS: managed more like DCIS (excision to clear margins)
  • DCIS: excision ± radiotherapy
  • Invasive cancer: surgery + adjuvant therapy by stage
exam_pearl: Do not treat classic LCIS like DCIS: margins are irrelevant and no radiotherapy or mastectomy is needed.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a history of severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain and yellow sclera. On examination, she appears unwell and has marked right upper quadrant tenderness with no guarding. An abdominal ultrasound reveals multiple gallstones and a dilated common bile duct (CBD) measuring 12 mm. She is initiated on intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Labs: White Blood Cells (WBC): 15.0 × 10⁹/L (high); Total Bilirubin: 43 µmol/L (high); Alkaline Phosphatase: 280 IU/L (high)
highlight_terms_source: dilated common bile duct (CBD) measuring 12 mm
why_right: RUQ pain, yellow sclera, cholestatic labs (high bilirubin and ALP) and gallstones with a 12 mm CBD mean an obstructing CBD stone, and the raised WBC in an unwell patient points to early cholangitis. With a high probability of a duct stone, ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic: it clears the duct and decompresses the biliary tree after fluids and antibiotics are started. Cholecystectomy follows once the duct is cleared.
why_wrong_block:
B. Emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy treats acute cholecystitis; done alone it leaves the obstructing CBD stone, so the duct must be cleared first.
C. MRCP only diagnoses; it is chosen when the chance of a CBD stone is intermediate (e.g. abnormal LFTs with a normal-calibre duct). Here a dilated duct plus jaundice already makes a stone highly likely and therapy is needed.
D. Percutaneous cholecystostomy drains the gallbladder in acute cholecystitis when the patient is too sick for surgery; it does not relieve a blocked CBD.
key_concept:
Gallstones + dilated CBD + cholestasis = CBD stone: clear it by ERCP, then cholecystectomy.
  • Charcot triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice) = cholangitis: resuscitate, antibiotics, ERCP decompression
  • High probability of CBD stone: ERCP directly
  • Intermediate probability: MRCP or EUS first
  • ERCP fails or not available: percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
  • Acute cholecystitis in a patient unfit for surgery: percutaneous cholecystostomy
exam_pearl: Jaundice plus a dilated CBD changes the target from the gallbladder to the duct: think ERCP, not cholecystectomy or cholecystostomy.

stem: child i think 18month came for vaccinations, mother reported hx of chicken pox infection 2 months ago that was CONFIRMED CLINICALLY, rash subsided within a few days, mother also showed a picture of the rash and it was consistent with varicella. whats the best action regarding varicella vaccination
why_right: Varicella that was confirmed clinically by a health care provider, with a rash consistent with varicella, counts as evidence of immunity. Natural infection gives lifelong immunity, so the varicella vaccine is not needed and should not be given; the rest of the schedule continues as normal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Give ivig: passive immunisation is for high-risk, non-immune contacts after exposure; this child is well and already immune.
B. Give vaccine now: right for a non-immune child at 12 to 15 months or a child with an uncertain history; a provider-verified episode makes vaccination unnecessary.
C. Give vaccine at 2 years: there is no reason to delay or schedule a varicella dose in a child who is already immune.
key_concept:
Evidence of varicella immunity means no vaccine.
  • Immunity: age-appropriate vaccine doses, provider-diagnosed or verified varicella or zoster, laboratory evidence of immunity
  • Uncertain or parent-only history: vaccinate
  • Routine schedule: 2 doses; susceptible 13 years or older: 2 doses 4 weeks apart
  • Live vaccine: avoid in immunocompromised children
exam_pearl: A clinically confirmed episode equals immunity; it is the unverified history that gets vaccinated.

stem: Baby for 9m vaccination, which of the following would be considered a contraindication for vaccination.
why_right: Among these, only a moderate to severe acute illness (with or without fever) is a reason to defer the 9-month vaccines until the child recovers. Mild illness, unrelated drug allergies and current medication are common misconceptions and do not justify withholding vaccines.
why_wrong_block:
B. Penicillin allergy: vaccines do not contain penicillin, so it is not a contraindication; only anaphylaxis to a vaccine component or a prior dose is.
C. Pharmacological therapy: current antibiotics or most other drugs do not stop vaccination; the exceptions are immunosuppressive therapy (avoid live vaccines) and recent blood products (delay MMR and varicella).
key_concept:
True contraindications are few; most reasons to delay are myths.
  • Contraindication: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component
  • Defer: moderate or severe acute illness
  • Live vaccines: avoid in immunocompromise and pregnancy
  • Not contraindications: mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotics, local reactions, unrelated allergies (penicillin)
exam_pearl: Moderate to severe illness is technically a precaution (defer), but it is the only listed option that changes the plan.

stem: A pic of rooting relfex, when will it disappear ?
why_right: The picture shows the rooting reflex: stroking the side of the mouth makes the infant turn toward and follow the stimulus. It is present from birth and disappears by about 4 months, as feeding becomes voluntary. Persistence beyond this age suggests a CNS problem.
why_wrong_block:
A. 2 months is too early for rooting; the asymmetrical tonic neck (fencing) reflex is the one that fades around 2 to 3 months.
C. 6 months is when the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes disappear, not rooting.
D. Rooting should be long gone by 8 months; this is around when the parachute reflex appears (a protective reflex that persists for life).
key_concept:
Primitive reflexes disappear in a predictable order; persistence or asymmetry is abnormal.
  • ATNR (fencing): about 2 to 3 months
  • Rooting and Galant: about 4 months
  • Moro and palmar grasp: about 6 months
  • Babinski (upgoing): until 12 to 18 months
  • Parachute: appears 8 to 10 months, never disappears
exam_pearl: Rooting = 4 months; do not confuse with Moro/grasp (6 months) or ATNR (2 to 3 months) when the picture is of the mouth.

stem: An 82-year-old man hospitalized for a severe urinary tract infection develops acute confusion, agitation, and a fluctuating level of consciousness. He is diagnosed with delirium. In addition to treating his underlying infection, what is the most appropriate next step in his supportive management?
OptB: Reorient the patient frequently to time and place
OptC: Apply physical restraints to prevent accidental falls
OptD: Place the patient in a dark, completely isolated room
highlight_terms_source: acute confusion, agitation, and a fluctuating level of consciousness
why_right: Delirium is managed by treating the cause (here the UTI) plus non-pharmacological supportive care, which is first line. Frequent reorientation to time and place (clocks, calendars, familiar faces), a calm lit room by day, normal sleep cycle, glasses and hearing aids reduce confusion and agitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Initiate low-dose haloperidol therapy: reserved for severe agitation that endangers the patient or staff after non-drug measures fail; not routine supportive care.
C. Apply physical restraints to prevent accidental falls: restraints increase agitation, injury and delirium duration; use only as a last resort for immediate danger.
D. Place the patient in a dark, completely isolated room: sensory deprivation and isolation worsen disorientation; the room should be well lit by day with familiar people present.
key_concept:
Delirium management ladder:
  • 1. Find and treat the cause (infection, drugs, metabolic)
  • 2. Non-drug measures: reorientation, family, glasses/hearing aids, sleep hygiene, mobilization
  • 3. Low-dose antipsychotic only for dangerous agitation
  • Avoid restraints, benzodiazepines (except alcohol withdrawal) and isolation
exam_pearl: "Supportive management" in delirium means reorientation; haloperidol is the trap unless agitation is dangerous.

stem: A 9 month baby, with 6 months bone age, GH is normal, IGF 1 is low
why_right: This recall mirrors the classic case of a 9-year-old with bone age 6 (the "months" in the stem are most likely a garbled "years"). A bone age delayed by 2 years or more points to a pathological cause, and a normal random GH with low IGF-1 shows inadequate GH action, since IGF-1 is produced in response to GH. Random GH is pulsatile and unreliable, so the low IGF-1 is the telling result, classified here as GH deficiency.
why_wrong_block:
A. Failure to thrive is weight faltering from poor intake or illness; it would show weight dropping across centiles first, not an isolated low IGF-1 with a delayed bone age.
B. Constitutional delay also has a delayed bone age, but IGF-1 is appropriate for bone age and growth velocity is normal, with a family history of late puberty; it would be right if labs were normal and a parent was a late bloomer.
key_concept:
Short stature: bone age plus IGF-1 sorts the causes.
  • Familial: bone age = chronological age, short parents, normal IGF-1
  • Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, normal velocity, family history of late puberty
  • GH deficiency: bone age delayed (often ≥2 years), low IGF-1, poor velocity
  • Confirm GH deficiency with GH stimulation testing
exam_pearl: A normal random GH does not exclude GH deficiency; low IGF-1 is the screening clue.

stem: A 14-year-old boy presents to the pediatric clinic complaining of recurrent crampy abdominal pain, persistent non-bloody diarrhea, and weight loss over the past 3 months. A colonoscopy is performed and reveals deep, longitudinal mucosal ulcerations alternating with areas of completely normal-appearing mucosa, alongside multiple aphthous ulcers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Chronic non-bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and weight loss in a teenager suggest IBD, and the colonoscopy decides the type. Deep longitudinal ulcers alternating with completely normal mucosa are skip lesions with a cobblestone pattern, and aphthous ulcers are early Crohn's lesions. This patchy, transmural pattern is Crohn's disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ulcerative colitis gives continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum upward with no skip areas, and usually bloody diarrhea with urgency; it would be right with bloody stools and diffuse friable mucosa.
C. Celiac disease is a small bowel disease seen on duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy) with positive tTG antibodies; it does not produce colonic ulceration.
D. Pseudomembranous colitis follows antibiotic use and shows yellow-white plaques (pseudomembranes) from C. difficile, with an acute course rather than 3 months of weight loss.
key_concept:
Crohn's vs UC is decided by distribution and depth.
  • Crohn's: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural, cobblestoning, granulomas, fistulas, strictures, often non-bloody
  • UC: rectum upward, continuous, mucosal only, bloody diarrhea, pseudopolyps
  • Aphthous ulcers and perianal disease favour Crohn's
exam_pearl: "Normal mucosa between ulcers" = skip lesions = Crohn's; continuous involvement from the rectum = UC.

stem: Male patient in his 20s, present with sever epigastric pain for 6 hours, start suddenly. On examination there is diffuse tenderness, sluggish bowel sound. Labs: high WBCs, Amylase 300 Which of the following best initial diagnostic step?
highlight_terms_source: sever epigastric pain for 6 hours, start suddenly
why_right: Sudden severe epigastric pain for 6 hours with diffuse tenderness and sluggish bowel sounds in a young man suggests a perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis. The best initial test is an erect chest X-ray, which quickly shows free air under the diaphragm. A modest amylase rise such as 300 can occur with perforation and does not by itself establish pancreatitis, so free air must be excluded first.
why_wrong_block:
B. Abdominal X-ray is less sensitive for small amounts of free air; it is the first film when bowel obstruction (distension, vomiting, colicky pain) is the main concern.
C. Abdominal CT is the confirmatory test when plain films are inconclusive or to assess pancreatitis severity, but it is not the initial step.
D. Abdominal US is first for biliary pain or gallstone pancreatitis; gas limits it and it is poor for detecting free air.
key_concept:
Sudden severe epigastric pain + peritonism: erect CXR first to look for free air.
  • Free air: perforated viscus, go to laparotomy (duodenal ulcer: omental patch)
  • Amylase or lipase ≥ 3 times the upper limit + typical pain: pancreatitis
  • Diagnosis unclear after plain films: CT abdomen
  • Suspected gallstone cause: abdominal US
exam_pearl: A mildly raised amylase in sudden epigastric pain is a trap: perforation can raise it too, so get the erect CXR first.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric endocrine clinic by his mother due to concerns regarding his short stature. On physical examination, his height and weight are both tracking steadily along the 3rd percentile, and his systemic exam is otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation reveals a normal random TSH , FSH , but a low insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) level for his chronological age. A left wrist radiograph demonstrates a bone age of 6 years. Upon taking the family history, the physician notes that the mother short. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
why_right: Height on the 3rd centile with a bone age of 6 at age 9 is a 3-year delay, and a delay of 2 years or more points to a pathological cause. The low IGF-1 with otherwise normal pituitary tests (TSH, FSH) localises the problem to the GH axis. A short mother is a distractor: familial short stature does not lower IGF-1 or delay bone age.
why_wrong_block:
B. Familial short stature has a bone age equal to chronological age and normal IGF-1; it would be right if bone age were 9 with normal labs and short parents.
C. Nutritional failure to thrive affects weight before height and the child is usually thin with abnormal exam; here weight and height track together and the exam is normal.
D. Constitutional delay also shows a delayed bone age, but IGF-1 is normal for bone age and there is a family history of late puberty; the low IGF-1 points away from it.
key_concept:
Short child: check bone age, growth velocity and IGF-1.
  • Bone age normal + short parents: familial
  • Bone age delayed + normal IGF-1 + late-bloomer parent: constitutional
  • Bone age delayed ≥2 years + low IGF-1: GH deficiency (confirm with stimulation test, treat with GH)
exam_pearl: A short mother tempts "familial", but a delayed bone age plus low IGF-1 overrides family history.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Question repeated verbatim as a 'Q:' restatement below the answer (no separate answer).

stem: An unvaccinated child develops a high-grade fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a maculopapular rash that started behind the ears and spread downward to the trunk. On oral examination, small gray-white spots on an erythematous base (Koplik spots) are noted on the buccal mucosa. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Supportive and conservative care (fluids and antipyretics)
highlight_terms_source: behind the ears and spread downward
why_right: High fever with the 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots and a rash starting behind the ears and spreading downward is measles in an unvaccinated child. Measles is viral with no specific antiviral, so management is supportive: fluids, antipyretics and monitoring for complications. Vitamin A supplementation is also recommended for children with measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV acyclovir treats HSV and serious varicella infections; it has no activity against measles virus. It would be right for neonatal HSV or varicella in an immunocompromised child.
C. Antibiotics do not treat a viral illness; they are used only when a secondary bacterial complication such as pneumonia or otitis media develops.
key_concept:
Measles = clinical diagnosis, supportive treatment.
  • Prodrome: fever + cough, coryza, conjunctivitis
  • Koplik spots (pathognomonic) precede the rash
  • Rash: behind ears/face, spreads downward
  • Treatment: supportive + vitamin A; isolate
  • Complications: pneumonia (commonest cause of death), otitis media, encephalitis, SSPE years later
exam_pearl: Antivirals and antibiotics are traps in uncomplicated measles; add antibiotics only for a proven bacterial complication.

stem: Child with increasing jaundice, flapping tremor and decreased school performance. O/E stigmata of chronic liver disease are present. Which of the following is MOST APPROPRIATE management?
highlight_terms_source: increasing jaundice, flapping tremor and decreased school performance
why_wrong_block:
A. Liver biopsy (with hepatic copper measurement) can confirm Wilson disease, but it is an invasive diagnostic step and risky in a decompensated, likely coagulopathic child; it is not management.
B. A HIDA scan assesses biliary excretion (for example biliary atresia or acute cholecystitis); it does not address chronic liver disease with encephalopathy.
C. 24-hour urinary copper is a supportive diagnostic test for Wilson disease (with low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings), but the question asks for management, not diagnosis.
key_concept:
Wilson disease: liver + brain + eyes in a young patient.
  • Liver: hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure
  • CNS: tremor, rigidity, behavioural change, falling school performance
  • Eyes: Kayser-Fleischer rings
  • Labs: low ceruloplasmin, high 24h urinary copper
  • Treatment: chelation (D-penicillamine), zinc for maintenance; liver transplant for fulminant or decompensated disease
exam_pearl: "Most appropriate management" asks for treatment; the three listed options are all investigations.
compiler_note:
⚠ Page lists only options A-C (liver biopsy, HIDA scan, 24h urinary copper) but prints 'Answer: D'; endorsed option does not exist on the page. Card mirrors this (answer 'D' with no D option).
Compiler note: Answer line says D, but only options A-C are printed (option D missing from the recall).

stem: A young male presents after a motorcycle trauma. On examination, there is blood at the urethral meatus. Pelvic X-ray reveals a pelvic fracture. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. What is the initial investigation?
why_right: Blood at the urethral meatus with a pelvic fracture means a urethral injury until proven otherwise. The initial investigation is a retrograde urethrogram, done before any urethral catheter is passed, because blind catheterisation can turn a partial tear into a complete one. He is haemodynamically stable (BP 110/70), so there is no bleeding emergency to address first.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI pelvis is too slow for acute trauma and is used later to plan delayed urethral reconstruction, not for the initial diagnosis.
B. CT with contrast is used in a stable patient to assess pelvic and visceral injuries (and CT cystography for bladder injury), but it does not reliably show the urethra; the urethrogram answers the question raised by meatal blood.
C. Pelvic angiography (with embolisation) is for an unstable patient with ongoing pelvic arterial bleeding; this patient is stable.
key_concept:
Urethral injury: RUG first, then suprapubic catheter; never a Foley first.
  • Clues: blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, perineal or scrotal haematoma, inability to void
  • Most commonly injured with pelvic fracture: posterior (membranous) urethra
  • RUG confirms injury: suprapubic cystostomy for drainage
  • Unstable pelvic fracture: pelvic binder, then angioembolisation or packing
exam_pearl: Blood at the meatus forbids a urethral catheter: RUG comes first, then a suprapubic catheter if injured.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (option d bold/underlined); compiler: Answer: D. Retrograde Urethrogram.

stem: calculate the ASA score. hypertension, not very controlled, mildly elevated, diabetes (can’t rememembr on metformin or insulin). 2 years ago had inferior stemi, not managed with a stent but he took aspirin and statin. now coming for an elective inguinal hernia repair, what's the ASA score
why_right: ASA III is severe systemic disease that limits function but is not a constant threat to life. This patient has poorly controlled hypertension, diabetes and a previous MI 2 years ago; uncontrolled HTN or DM and a history of MI more than 3 months before surgery each place a patient in ASA III. His elective hernia repair does not change the class, which describes the patient, not the operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. ASA 1 is a normal healthy patient with no systemic disease; this patient has several.
B. ASA 2 is mild, well-controlled systemic disease (e.g. controlled DM or HTN alone); his poorly controlled HTN and prior MI push him higher.
D. ASA 4 is severe disease that is a constant threat to life, such as an MI within the last 3 months, ongoing ischaemia or decompensated heart failure; his MI was 2 years ago and he is stable.
key_concept:
ASA class = patient's physical status, independent of the planned surgery.
  • I: healthy
  • II: mild controlled disease (controlled DM or HTN, smoker, mild obesity)
  • III: severe disease (poorly controlled DM or HTN, MI more than 3 months ago, morbid obesity)
  • IV: constant threat to life (recent MI, ongoing ischaemia)
  • V: moribund, not expected to survive without surgery
  • VI: brain dead organ donor; add E for emergency
exam_pearl: Controlled DM = II, but uncontrolled disease or any past MI moves the patient to III; recent MI (within 3 months) makes it IV.

stem: a guy fell from 4 stories. has a double fracture in the third fourth and fifth ribs with lung contusion. Breath sounds present. What’s the next best step
highlight_terms_source: double fracture in the third fourth and fifth ribs
why_right: Ribs 3, 4 and 5 each broken in two places is a flail segment with an underlying lung contusion, and breath sounds are present, so there is no pneumothorax or haemothorax to drain. Management is supportive, and the cornerstone is adequate analgesia (often regional), which allows deep breathing and coughing and prevents hypoventilation and pneumonia. Oxygen, physiotherapy and careful fluids follow; ventilation is added only if he becomes hypoxic or tires.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgical rib fixation is reserved for selected flail chest (failure to wean from the ventilator, severe chest wall instability or deformity), not as the next step in a patient breathing on his own.
C. A chest tube treats a pneumothorax or haemothorax; preserved breath sounds give no reason to place one.
D. Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, hypotension, tracheal shift), none of which is described.
key_concept:
Flail chest + contusion: treat the lung and the pain, not the ribs.
  • Flail chest: 3 or more adjacent ribs each fractured in 2 or more places, paradoxical movement
  • First line: analgesia, oxygen, physiotherapy, avoid fluid overload
  • Hypoxia or respiratory failure: assisted ventilation
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
  • Simple pneumothorax or haemothorax: chest tube
exam_pearl: If the stem adds hypoxia (low SpO2) to the flail chest, the answer shifts to assisted ventilation.

stem: A 27-year-old man sustains a single gunshot wound to the left thigh. In the ER, he is noted to have a large hematoma of his medial thigh. He complains of paresthesias in his left foot. On examination, there are weak pulses palpable distal to the injury and the patient is unable to move his foot. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this patient?
OptB: Immediate exploration and repair in the operating room
OptC: Fasciotomy of the anterior compartment of the calf
highlight_terms_source: gunshot wound to the left thigh
why_right: A penetrating thigh wound with a large hematoma, distal paresthesia and inability to move the foot shows a limb that is already ischaemic, even though weak pulses are palpable. These are hard signs of arterial injury, so the patient goes straight to the operating room for exploration and repair; delaying for imaging risks losing the limb. Any needed fasciotomy or on-table angiography is done during that operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Angiography (or CT angiography) is for soft signs only, such as a diminished pulse or small stable hematoma with a viable limb; with an ischaemic, paralysed foot it wastes time.
C. Fasciotomy is often added at the time of revascularisation to prevent reperfusion compartment syndrome, but on its own it does not fix the arterial injury causing the ischaemia.
D. Observation for spasm is never acceptable after penetrating trauma with ischaemic signs; a pulse deficit must be assumed to be an arterial injury.
E. Local wound exploration at the bedside is unsafe in a deep thigh wound with a large hematoma, because it can release uncontrolled bleeding without the means to control it.
key_concept:
Penetrating extremity trauma: hard signs go to the OR, soft signs get imaging.
  • Hard signs: pulsatile bleeding, expanding or pulsatile hematoma, absent pulses, bruit or thrill, distal ischaemia
  • Hard signs: immediate operative exploration and repair
  • Soft signs (diminished pulse, small stable hematoma, nearby nerve deficit, abnormal ABI): CT angiography
  • Prolonged ischaemia: add fasciotomy at the time of repair
exam_pearl: Palpable but weak pulses do not reassure you: a cold, numb, paralysed foot means ischaemia and the OR.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot; 'Answer: B 💯'. 'operating room' and 'bedside' highlighted in red in the source.

stem: 56 years old. on Aspirin and some other med. Presenting with 6 or 8 hrs of painless rectal bleed with clots. No abd pain, no weight loss, no changes in bowel movement, no abdominal tenderness. No hemorrhoids or masses seen. Whaat the most likely case
why_right: A 56-year-old on aspirin with an acute episode of painless rectal bleeding with clots, and no pain, weight loss, change in bowel habit or anorectal lesion, fits a vascular cause of lower GI bleeding. Among the listed options this is angiodysplasia, which typically gives painless, intermittent bleeding in older adults and is made worse by antiplatelets.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colon cancer usually causes slow, occult or low-volume bleeding with anaemia, weight loss or a change in bowel habit; a sudden clot-forming bleed without these features is less typical, though colonoscopy is still needed at this age.
C. IBD presents with bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, urgency and often weight loss, usually in younger patients; isolated painless bleeding does not fit.
key_concept:
Painless lower GI bleeding in an older adult = vascular cause.
  • Diverticulosis: the most common cause of painless large-volume bleeding (if listed)
  • Angiodysplasia: painless, often recurrent, older patients, associated with aortic stenosis and CKD
  • Colon cancer: occult bleeding, anaemia, weight loss, change in habit
  • IBD: bloody diarrhoea with pain in a younger patient
  • Haemorrhoids: bright red blood after defecation, seen on exam
exam_pearl: If diverticulosis is among the options it is usually preferred for painless large bleeding; without it, choose angiodysplasia.

stem: Pediatric pt with bronchiolitis treated conservatively with hydration and suction then develop fever 38 and loss of appetite and red pharynx. What will require further investigations?
why_right: Bronchiolitis and viral URTIs are managed supportively, and some fever with a red throat is part of the expected viral course. A fever that persists or rises instead of settling is the warning sign of a secondary bacterial infection (pneumonia, otitis media) or another diagnosis, so it is the finding that justifies further investigations such as a CBC or chest X-ray.
why_wrong_block: B. Pharyngeal erythema is a common, nonspecific finding in viral respiratory infections and by itself does not change management; it would matter only with features of bacterial pharyngitis (exudate, tender nodes, no cough).
key_concept:
Viral respiratory illness: investigate when the course deviates.
  • Expected: low-grade fever, coryza, cough, red throat, improvement over days
  • Red flags: persistent or high fever, worsening distress, hypoxia, poor feeding/dehydration, lethargy
  • Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis; routine tests are not needed
exam_pearl: Fever that persists beyond the expected viral course, not a red throat, prompts looking for a bacterial complication.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question as the numbered recall 'Kid with fever, runny nose, for a few days. Now not improving, fever persisting and throat erythematous what makes u do further investigation A. persisting fever B. red throat' (Answer: A). The 'Q:' restatement answers A. Persistent high fever (answer line on p574).

stem: Woman with neck mass showing hypo echoic with irregular borders
why_right: A neck (thyroid) nodule that is hypoechoic with irregular borders on ultrasound has suspicious features for malignancy. The next step is fine needle aspiration, and the result is reported with the Bethesda system, which then decides between follow-up, repeat FNA or surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Thyroidectomy is planned only after cytology: lobectomy for Bethesda IV (and some V), total or near-total thyroidectomy for Bethesda VI. Operating on imaging alone skips the diagnosis.
C. This option was not recalled; other plausible distractors are a TSH level (the first test in any nodule workup, scan if TSH is low) or ultrasound follow-up, which suits nodules without suspicious features.
key_concept:
Thyroid nodule: TSH + US, then FNA for suspicious features; Bethesda decides the rest.
  • Low TSH: isotope scan (hot nodule rarely malignant)
  • Suspicious US: hypoechoic, irregular margins, microcalcifications, taller than wide
  • Bethesda I or III: repeat FNA
  • Bethesda II: US follow-up
  • Bethesda IV: hemithyroidectomy
  • Bethesda VI: near-total or total thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: Never jump to thyroidectomy from imaging alone; cytology comes first unless TSH is low.

stem: A Patient Presents With Back Pain And Hypesthesia Localized To The Left Lateral Calf And Left Lateral Foot. Which Of The Following Nerve Root Levels Is Most Likely Affected?
highlight_terms_source: Left Lateral Calf And Left Lateral Foot
why_right: Numbness of the lateral calf follows the L5 dermatome and numbness of the lateral foot follows the S1 dermatome. The question asks which nerve roots are affected, and only the L5-S1 pair covers both areas. Back pain with this pattern fits lumbar radiculopathy (for example a disc or foraminal lesion compressing both roots).
why_wrong_block:
A. L3-L4 roots supply the anterior thigh, knee and medial leg (knee extension, knee reflex); they do not reach the lateral calf or lateral foot.
B. L4-L5 roots cover the medial leg (L4) and the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot (L5); the lateral foot (S1) would be spared.
D. S1-S2 roots cover the lateral foot (S1) and the posterior thigh and calf (S2); the lateral calf is L5, so this pair misses it.
key_concept:
Lower limb dermatomes: L4 medial leg, L5 lateral leg and dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot and sole.
  • L4: medial leg, knee extension, knee reflex
  • L5: lateral leg, dorsum of foot, big toe dorsiflexion, no reliable reflex
  • S1: lateral foot and little toe, plantarflexion, ankle reflex
  • S2: posterior thigh and calf
  • Lumbar disc usually compresses the root below (L4-L5 disc = L5 root, L5-S1 disc = S1 root)
exam_pearl: Lateral foot and little toe = S1 (sural territory); if only the dorsum of the foot is numb, think L5.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed version: 'Loss of sensation to lateral ankle and foot what nerve supple A. L3/L4 B. L4/L5 C. L5/S1 D. s1/s2 or s2/s3' (no answer line); answer taken from the attached screenshot (Answer: C).

stem: Hypoesthesia at left medial calf and left medial foot, which nerve root affected?
highlight_terms_source: left medial calf and left medial foot
why_right: Sensory loss over the "medial calf" and "medial foot" is the L4 dermatome, the same strip supplied by the saphenous nerve (L3 to L4). An L4 root is classically compressed by an L3-L4 disc, so that level fits the map. Medial = L4; this variant flips the lateral version of the same question.
why_wrong_block:
B. L4-L5: compresses the L5 root, giving numbness of the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot / big toe with weak big toe extension; the deficit here is medial, not dorsal.
C. L5-S1: compresses S1, giving numbness of the lateral foot, little toe and sole with a reduced ankle reflex; that is the lateral version of this question.
D. S1-S2: sacral roots supply the posterior calf, heel and lateral border of the foot (sural territory), not the medial leg.
key_concept:
Leg dermatomes: read the side of the leg, then name the root.
  • L4: medial leg and medial malleolus/medial foot; knee jerk; disc L3-L4
  • L5: lateral leg, dorsum of foot, big toe; big toe extension; disc L4-L5
  • S1: lateral foot, little toe, sole; ankle jerk; disc L5-S1
  • Saphenous nerve (L3 to L4): medial leg down to the medial foot
exam_pearl: Medial calf/foot = L4 (L3-L4); lateral foot = S1 (L5-S1): read which side the stem says before answering.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant screenshot shown under 2276 (medial rather than lateral).

stem: Concerned mom with her newborn ask about when is the time for screening for IDA:
why_right: Iron-deficiency anemia screening (Hb/CBC) is done for all infants at 9 to 12 months, because iron stores from birth are depleted by then and dietary intake is often inadequate. Of the options, 10 months is the only one inside this window. A repeat at 15 to 18 months is reserved for children with risk factors.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 2 months term infants still have iron stores from birth, so routine screening is not useful; physiological anemia of infancy is expected around this age.
B. At 4 months, stores are usually still adequate; 4 to 6 months is when iron supplementation or iron-rich complementary foods are started, especially in breastfed infants, not when screening is done.
D. 18 months is the optional repeat screen for at-risk children, not the universal first screen.
key_concept:
Well-baby screening timing.
  • IDA screen: 9 to 12 months (repeat 15 to 18 months if at risk)
  • Autism screen: about 18 to 24 months
  • Head circumference: up to 2 years
  • BMI: from 2 years
exam_pearl: Pick the age inside 9 to 12 months; 18 months is only the at-risk repeat.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler heading: Screening of IDA 9-12 months.

stem: Newborn delivered by vacuum, and had blood cross sutures (cephalohematoma), he had tachycardia and hypotension and Hb 7.5. What will you do?
why_right: A vacuum delivery with a scalp bleed that crosses the sutures is a subgaleal hemorrhage (the source calls it cephalohematoma, but a true cephalohematoma is limited by sutures and rarely causes shock). The subgaleal space can hold a large volume of blood, and tachycardia, hypotension and Hb 7.5 mean hemorrhagic shock. Management is volume replacement with IV fluids and blood transfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. FFP corrects clotting factor deficiency and may be added if a coagulopathy is found, but it does not replace lost red cells; it is not the primary treatment for hemorrhagic shock with Hb 7.5.
B. "Immediate resuscitation" is too vague; option C states the specific resuscitation this baby needs (volume plus red cells for blood-loss shock).
key_concept:
Neonatal scalp swellings after instrumental delivery.
  • Caput succedaneum: scalp edema, crosses sutures, present at birth, resolves in about 48 hours
  • Cephalohematoma: subperiosteal, limited by sutures, appears gradually, risk of jaundice
  • Subgaleal hemorrhage: under the aponeurosis, crosses sutures, fluctuant, can cause hypovolemic shock
  • Shock + falling Hb: fluids and blood transfusion, check coagulation
exam_pearl: Crossing sutures + shock after vacuum = subgaleal hemorrhage; treat the blood loss with transfusion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Blood crossing sutures actually suggests subgaleal hemorrhage (source labels it cephalohematoma).

stem: Pt presented with RUQ pain and vomiting. Vitals stable (I believe). The imaging showed thinking of the gallbladder and gallstones
highlight_terms_source: thinking of the gallbladder and gallstones
why_right: "RUQ pain and vomiting" with "thickening of the gallbladder and gallstones" on imaging is acute calculous cholecystitis. With stable vitals, definitive treatment is laparoscopic cholecystectomy, preferably early (within 72 hours of onset), after NPO, IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics. Nothing in the stem points to a stone in the common bile duct.
why_wrong_block: B. ERCP and sphincterotomy: treats choledocholithiasis or cholangitis, signalled by jaundice, raised bilirubin and ALP and a dilated CBD; here the stones and inflammation are in the gallbladder itself.
key_concept:
Gallstone disease: where the stone sits decides the procedure.
  • Biliary colic: short pain, normal wall; elective lap chole
  • Acute cholecystitis: prolonged pain, fever, Murphy sign, thick wall, pericholecystic fluid; early lap chole
  • High surgical risk or acalculous: percutaneous cholecystostomy
  • CBD stone (raised bilirubin/ALP, dilated CBD) or cholangitis: ERCP first, then cholecystectomy
exam_pearl: ERCP becomes the answer only when labs or imaging place the stone in the CBD.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'thinking' likely means thickening.

stem: A 33-year-old woman diagnosed with papillary thyroid cancer and planed for total thyroidectomy, she have mitral valve prolapse with mild regurgitation, no other co-morbidity. Which of the following is most appropriate option to prevent infection?
highlight_terms_source: mitral valve prolapse with mild regurgitation
why_right: Mitral valve prolapse with mild regurgitation is not a high-risk cardiac lesion, so endocarditis prophylaxis is not indicated, and thyroidectomy is not a high-risk procedure for endocarditis anyway. Total thyroidectomy is a clean operation without an implant, so routine wound-infection prophylaxis is not needed either. Hence no antibiotic prophylaxis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amoxicillin to prevent endocarditis: reserved for high-risk patients (prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease) undergoing high-risk procedures such as dental work with gingival manipulation; MVP does not qualify.
B. Cefazolin to prevent wound infection: right for clean-contaminated surgery or clean surgery with an implanted prosthesis/mesh; a thyroidectomy is clean and implant-free.
D. Both cefazolin and amoxicillin: neither indication is present, so combining them only adds side effects and resistance.
key_concept:
Endocarditis prophylaxis needs BOTH a high-risk heart AND a high-risk procedure.
  • High risk: prosthetic valve or prosthetic repair material, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-repaired congenital disease, valvulopathy in a transplanted heart
  • Not high risk: MVP with MR, bicuspid valve, acquired valve disease, simple ASD, HCM, rheumatic fever without valve dysfunction
  • Clean surgery without implant (thyroidectomy): no wound prophylaxis
exam_pearl: Even a prosthetic valve gets no prophylaxis for a procedure that is not high risk for IE.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Clean surgery; MVP not an endocarditis prophylaxis indication.

stem: 78-year-old male post-op contaminated abdominal surgery. Admitted to ICU and received 6 L of crystalloid IV fluid and 1 PRBC in the last 12 hours. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were administered. CVA 10 and urine output 20 ml/hr. Vitals: BP 70/45, HR: 125, T: 38.6, O2: 93%, Labs: WBC 8. What is the most appropriate IV intervention?
why_right: After contaminated surgery he has fever (38.6), tachycardia and BP 70/45 despite "6 L of crystalloid" and a unit of blood, with a CVP of 10 and oliguria: this is fluid-refractory septic shock. Once adequately filled, the next IV intervention is a vasopressor, and norepinephrine is first line, titrated to a MAP of at least 65. A normal WBC does not exclude sepsis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Albumin: may be added when very large crystalloid volumes are needed, but it does not reverse vasodilatory hypotension; the priority at a MAP in the 50s is a vasopressor.
B. 2 L crystalloid: fluid is right in early hypotension or oliguria with normal BP (fluid challenge); after 6 L and a CVP of 10, more fluid adds edema and lung injury without restoring pressure.
D. Furosemide: the low urine output is from renal hypoperfusion, not overload; a diuretic would worsen hypotension. Right only for confirmed fluid overload in a perfused patient.
key_concept:
Septic shock ladder: source control + antibiotics + fluids, then pressors.
  • Hypotension persisting after adequate fluid = septic shock: start norepinephrine
  • Target MAP ≥ 65
  • Add vasopressin if norepinephrine alone is insufficient
  • Oliguria with normal BP after surgery: fluid challenge first
  • Look again for the source (anastomotic leak/collection) after contaminated surgery
exam_pearl: Large volume already given + still hypotensive = stop pushing fluid and start norepinephrine.
compiler_note: Compiler note: CVA likely means CVP.

stem: A patient presented after MVA with paraplegia and T6 injury, he is breathing well but his BP is 70/40. What is your initial step?
why_right: He is "breathing well", so airway and breathing are secured and the problem is Circulation: BP 70/40. A T6 cord injury can cause neurogenic shock, but hypotension after trauma must be treated (and hemorrhage excluded) first, and the initial step for either cause is isotonic IV fluid. Vasopressors are added if neurogenic hypotension persists after adequate fluid.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate intubation: indicated for SpO2 below 88%, GCS 8 or less, or aspiration risk, or a high cervical injury with failing breathing; a T6 lesion spares the diaphragm and he is breathing well.
C. CT: the best imaging to clear spinal and abdominal injuries, but only after the patient is hemodynamically stabilised; a BP of 70/40 belongs in resuscitation, not the scanner.
key_concept:
Trauma with hypotension: ABC in order; fix C before imaging.
  • Neurogenic shock: injury at or above T6, hypotension with bradycardia, warm dry skin
  • Hemorrhagic shock: tachycardia, cold clammy skin; always exclude first
  • Treatment: isotonic fluids first, then vasopressors if still hypotensive
  • Imaging (CT) once stable
exam_pearl: Paraplegia gives a reason for hypotension, not permission to skip looking for bleeding.

stem: Mixed thyroid, cystic and solid
key_concept:
Thyroid nodule: TSH first, then ultrasound-guided FNA of the suspicious (solid) component.
  • Low TSH: thyroid scan plus ultrasound before FNA
  • Mixed cystic-solid: sample the solid part
  • Bethesda IV: hemithyroidectomy on the affected side
  • Benign colloid nodule: no further action
  • Nodule under 1 cm: follow-up imaging
exam_pearl: Cyst fluid is low yield: the malignancy risk lives in the solid component.

stem: An 80-year-old man with Alzheimer disease has recently started wandering at night and sometimes leaves the house while asleep/confused. What is the most appropriate management?
OptA: Lock the doors and prevent him from leaving the house
OptB: Install door alarms and motion sensors
OptC: Buy a tracking device and attach it to him
key_concept:
Behavioral symptoms of dementia: non-drug first.
  • Identify triggers (pain, toileting, hunger, day-night reversal)
  • Daytime activity and sleep hygiene
  • Safety: alarms, sensors, identification, supervision
  • Drugs only for dangerous agitation or psychosis
exam_pearl: Antipsychotics for wandering are a trap; they add mortality risk without treating the behavior.

stem: A 37y patient suffered from circumferential right forearm burn + weak distal pulsation + oxygen saturation 86% in right arm, what is most appropriate next step
OptC: IV fluids, burn dressing, limb elevation
why_right: A "circumferential" full-thickness forearm burn forms an inelastic eschar that acts as a tourniquet as edema builds. "Weak distal pulsation" and low limb oxygen saturation (86%) show established vascular compromise, so the next step is immediate escharotomy to release the constriction. The diagnosis is clinical; nothing should delay release.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV vasodilators: the ischemia is mechanical compression by eschar, not vasospasm; dilators cannot overcome an external constriction and may drop systemic BP.
C. IV fluids, burn dressing, limb elevation: routine care for every burn and enough for a non-circumferential burn with good perfusion; once pulses fade it does not relieve the eschar.
D. Measure intracompartmental pressure: useful when deep muscle compartment syndrome is suspected but equivocal, e.g. after escharotomy fails or in electrical/crush injury; here perfusion is clearly compromised and measuring only delays release.
key_concept:
Circumferential full-thickness burn: watch distal perfusion.
  • Limb with weak pulses, low SpO2, cold or numb distally: escharotomy
  • Chest circumferential burn restricting ventilation: chest escharotomy
  • Persistent ischemia after escharotomy, or electrical/crush injury: fasciotomy (compartment syndrome)
  • Eschar is insensate, so escharotomy needs little anesthesia
exam_pearl: Escharotomy releases the skin; fasciotomy releases the muscle compartment. Burns usually need the first.

stem: Question about ruptured appendicitis, only mentions presence of abdominal pain and fever, no specific temperature, no size of abscess, asked about most appropriate next step:
key_concept:
Perforated appendicitis: peritonitis operates, containment waits.
  • Uncomplicated appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Perforation with generalized peritonitis: IV antibiotics + urgent appendectomy
  • Appendiceal abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics, then interval appendectomy
  • Phlegmon: IV antibiotics, conservative
  • CT defines complicated appendicitis at any age
exam_pearl: The words "abscess" or "mass" switch the answer from immediate surgery to drain/antibiotics then interval appendectomy.

stem: Adult involved in MVA with irregular breathing low bp and pulse (cushing's triad) but oriented and cannt move his limbs what to do?
why_right: A conscious patient who "cannot move his limbs" after an MVA with irregular/shallow breathing has a high cervical cord injury with impending respiratory failure, so the airway must be secured. The method of choice is orotracheal intubation (rapid sequence) with manual in-line stabilisation of the neck; a suspected C-spine injury is not a contraindication. Low BP with a slow pulse here reflects neurogenic shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tracheostomy: a planned procedure for prolonged ventilation (common later in high cord injury), not an emergency airway.
B. Cricothyroidotomy: the emergency surgical airway when orotracheal intubation fails or is impossible, e.g. severe maxillofacial injury or profuse oral bleeding; not first line here.
D. Nasotracheal tube: less reliable, needs spontaneous breathing, and is contraindicated with midface or basal skull fractures; it is not the preferred trauma airway.
key_concept:
Trauma airway: orotracheal intubation with in-line stabilisation is the default.
  • Intubate for: SpO2 below 88%, GCS 8 or less, aspiration risk, high cord injury with failing breathing
  • Facial/mandibular fracture or failed intubation: cricothyroidotomy
  • Tracheostomy: later, for prolonged ventilation
  • Cushing triad (raised ICP) = hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing; hypotension + bradycardia after cord injury = neurogenic shock
exam_pearl: C-spine injury does not push you to a surgical airway: intubate orally with manual in-line stabilisation.

Compiler's 'Q:' restatement (same question, same options, Answer: C): A trauma patient presents with quadriplegia (unable to move arms and legs), is conscious and oriented, but has shallow breathing.
