stem: A 25 years old woman presents with sever acne following with a dermatologist who prescribed her ISOTRETINOIN and advised her not to get pregnant. She asks when she can try to get pregnant, what is the most appropriate (counseling?) regarding her pregnancy?
OptA: The medication is safe to take during pregnancy
OptB: She can try to get pregnant after she finishes the treatment
OptC: Stop and try to get pregnant immediately
OptD: She can try to get pregnant after 3 months of stoping the medication
highlight_terms_source: when she can try to get pregnant
why_right: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen, so the counseling must include a drug free waiting period after the last dose before trying to conceive. Option D is the only choice that builds in a washout after stopping the medication; every other option allows pregnancy on the drug or with no interval. This recall's key is the 3 month interval.
why_wrong_block:
A. The medication is safe to take during pregnancy: false; isotretinoin causes severe craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations and is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
B. She can try to get pregnant after she finishes the treatment: omits the required drug free interval after the last dose, so conception could occur while the drug is still present.
C. Stop and try to get pregnant immediately: no washout period at all; conception must wait after the last dose.
key_concept:
Isotretinoin: teratogen requiring pregnancy prevention before, during and after treatment.
  • Pregnancy test before starting and during treatment
  • Effective contraception during therapy
  • Drug free wait after the last dose before conception (this recall keys 3 months)
  • Teratogenic effects: craniofacial, cardiac, thymic and CNS defects
  • Acitretin is the retinoid with a much longer post treatment interval (years)
  • Pregnancy on isotretinoin: stop the drug and refer for counseling
exam_pearl: Never 'immediately' or 'once treatment ends': isotretinoin counseling always includes a drug free wait after the last dose.

stem: A female patient on isotretinoin for Acne. wishes to conceive. What should the physician tell her about the appropriate time?
OptA: She can conceive as soon as she stops the isotretinoin
OptB: She can conceive while taking isotretinoin
OptC: She can conceive after 3 months off of isotretinoin
OptD: She can conceive after 1 month of stopping isotretinoin
why_right: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic but has a short half life, so conception should wait until it has cleared. Current pregnancy prevention guidance asks women to avoid pregnancy for 1 month after stopping, which makes D the correct counseling on the appropriate time to conceive.
why_wrong_block:
A. She can conceive as soon as she stops the isotretinoin: no washout; conception must wait 1 month after the last dose.
B. She can conceive while taking isotretinoin: absolutely contraindicated; isotretinoin causes severe craniofacial, cardiac and CNS malformations.
C. She can conceive after 3 months off isotretinoin: overly long for isotretinoin; long post treatment intervals apply to acitretin, not isotretinoin.
key_concept:
Isotretinoin: avoid pregnancy during treatment and for 1 month after the last dose.
  • Negative pregnancy test before starting and monthly during treatment
  • Effective contraception during therapy and for 1 month after
  • Teratogenic effects: craniofacial, cardiac, thymic and CNS defects
  • Acitretin: much longer post treatment avoidance (years)
exam_pearl: Isotretinoin is 1 month; do not confuse it with acitretin's years long wait.

stem: Post MVA pt was hypotensive and tachycardic, ct scan was done and showed “large internal pelvic hematoma actively bleeding” most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: large internal pelvic hematoma actively bleeding
why_right: The patient is in haemorrhagic shock ("hypotensive and tachycardic") from an "actively bleeding" pelvic hematoma, so the immediate priority is circulation: restore volume with blood products (massive transfusion protocol) while the pelvis is stabilised. Pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal, so it is controlled by a pelvic binder, angioembolization or preperitoneal packing, not by opening the peritoneal cavity. Of the two options, transfusion is the correct management.
why_wrong_block: A. Ex lap does not reach a retroperitoneal pelvic bleed and opening the abdomen can release the tamponade and worsen the bleeding. It is right when the unstable trauma patient has intraperitoneal bleeding (positive FAST / free intraperitoneal blood).
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic bleeding: resuscitate and control the pelvis, do not laparotomise.
  • Circulation first: large-bore access, blood products (balanced transfusion)
  • Pelvic binder to close the pelvic volume
  • Arterial bleed on CT (contrast blush): angioembolization
  • Venous / unstable and no angio: preperitoneal packing ± external fixation
  • Positive FAST + unstable: laparotomy is for the abdomen, not the pelvis
exam_pearl: Pelvic hematoma = retroperitoneal: binder and embolization, not ex lap; free intraperitoneal blood in an unstable patient = ex lap.

stem: 40-50? year-old man undergoes colonoscopy, which reveals a 1.5 cm polyp in the colon Histopathology: Tubular Adenoma found and removed completely. When should the next colonoscopy screening be performed?
why_right: A tubular adenoma of "1.5 cm" is 10 mm or larger, which makes it an advanced adenoma (size alone qualifies, even with tubular histology). After complete removal of an advanced adenoma, surveillance colonoscopy is repeated at 3 years. The "removed completely" clue rules out an early re-look for incomplete resection.
why_wrong_block:
A. 3 to 6 months is for a large polyp removed piecemeal or incompletely, to check the resection site; here it was removed completely.
C. 10 years is the interval after a normal colonoscopy (average-risk screening) or for small hyperplastic polyps, not after an advanced adenoma.
D. An adenoma is a premalignant lesion, so surveillance is always needed; stopping screening is never right after an adenoma in a man of this age.
key_concept:
Post-polypectomy interval depends on size, number and histology.
  • Normal colonoscopy: 10 years
  • Small hyperplastic polyps: 10 years
  • 1 to 2 small tubular adenomas (<10 mm): 7 to 10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous component or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal removal of a large polyp: 6 months
  • Malignant risk: villous > tubulovillous > tubular > hyperplastic
exam_pearl: Size ≥1 cm makes even a tubular adenoma "advanced": 3 years, not 10.

stem: A guy with severe perineal pain and swelling, discoloration that is expanding with crepitus, what is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Severe perineal pain with swelling, skin "discoloration that is expanding" and "crepitus" is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia, i.e. Fournier's gangrene. Crepitus reflects gas from polymicrobial (including anaerobic) infection in the deep tissues, and rapid spread with violaceous skin marks necrosis. It is a surgical emergency treated with urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cellulitis gives redness, warmth and pain after minor trauma but no crepitus and no rapidly spreading dusky discoloration; pain out of proportion plus crepitus means necrotizing infection.
B. Testicular torsion presents with sudden testicular pain, a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex, usually in an adolescent; it does not cause perineal crepitus or spreading skin necrosis.
key_concept:
Perineal pain + spreading discoloration + crepitus = Fournier gangrene.
  • Necrotizing fasciitis of perineum, scrotum/penis (labia in females)
  • Polymicrobial: gram positive, gram negative, anaerobes
  • Clues: pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, violaceous skin, systemic toxicity
  • Treatment: urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
  • Untreated mortality is high
exam_pearl: Crepitus is the word that converts "cellulitis" into necrotizing infection needing the theatre.

stem: A 14-year-old patient presented with a painless neck swelling. Examination confirmed a midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone that moves up and down with swallowing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone
moves up and down with swallowing
why_right: A painless "midline" swelling "below the hyoid" that "moves up and down with swallowing" in a young patient is a thyroglossal cyst. It arises from a remnant of the thyroglossal duct, which is attached to the hyoid, so it moves with swallowing and classically also with tongue protrusion. Treatment is surgical excision (Sistrunk operation, including the central hyoid).
why_wrong_block:
A. Cystic hygroma is a lateral (posterior triangle) soft, transilluminating lymphatic mass, usually seen in infancy; it is not midline and does not move with swallowing.
C. A midline dermoid cyst is also midline but is not attached to the hyoid, so it does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion; it is often more superficial or submental.
D. Submental lymph nodes lie above the hyoid, are often tender when reactive and do not move with swallowing.
key_concept:
Midline neck mass: does it move with swallowing / tongue protrusion?
  • Moves with tongue protrusion and swallowing, at/below hyoid: thyroglossal cyst
  • Moves with swallowing only: thyroid nodule / goiter
  • Midline, no movement: dermoid cyst
  • Lateral, transilluminates, infant: cystic hygroma
  • Lateral, anterior to SCM: branchial cyst
exam_pearl: Movement with TONGUE PROTRUSION separates thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule, which moves only with swallowing.

stem: A 19-year-old woman 23-week pregnant primigravida presents with a complaint of irregular brownish patches of varying sizes on face and neck (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 23 week primigravida with irregular brownish patches on the face and neck has hormone driven facial hyperpigmentation of pregnancy. When this pattern appears in pregnancy it is called chloasma (the 'mask of pregnancy'), which is the term this recall keys. It is caused by estrogen and progesterone stimulating melanocytes and is worsened by sun exposure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Melasma: the same pigmentary process (chloasma is melasma occurring in pregnancy); the recall prefers the pregnancy specific term, while melasma fits a non pregnant woman, for example on oral contraceptives.
C. Tinea nigra: a painless brown to black macule, usually single, on the palms or soles; it does not cause symmetric facial patches.
D. Lichen planus: itchy, purple, polygonal, flat topped papules with Wickham striae on wrists, shins and oral mucosa; not brown facial patches.
key_concept:
Brown facial patches in pregnancy = chloasma (melasma of pregnancy).
  • Sites: cheeks, forehead, upper lip, nose
  • Cause: estrogen and progesterone stimulating melanocytes; worse with sun
  • Often fades after delivery; may persist
  • Management: sun protection and reassurance in pregnancy
  • Other pregnancy pigment changes: linea nigra, darkened areolae
exam_pearl: Same lesion, two names: in pregnancy the exam wants chloasma.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'B. Chloasma (MG)'. Image referenced but not shown on page.

stem: Acute mesenteric ischemia history of ischemic stroke 1 month ago what is the initial management ?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the "initial management" of acute mesenteric ischemia. The first step is resuscitation and anticoagulation: IV fluids for the third-space losses and IV unfractionated heparin to stop clot propagation, before imaging (CT angiography) and revascularization. The "ischemic stroke 1 month ago" also points to an embolic source and contraindicates thrombolysis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Angiography with embolectomy is the definitive treatment for embolic mesenteric ischemia, but it follows resuscitation and heparin; it is not the initial step.
B. Thrombolysis is contraindicated here because of an ischemic stroke within the last 3 months, and it is not the first step anyway; catheter-directed lysis is reserved for selected early cases without peritonitis.
D. Abdominal ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and does not show the mesenteric vessels adequately; CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice.
key_concept:
Acute mesenteric ischemia: resuscitate, anticoagulate, image, revascularize.
  • Clue: elderly, AF/MI/recent embolic event, pain out of proportion to exam
  • Labs: leukocytosis, lactic acidosis
  • Initial: IV fluids + IV heparin (+ broad-spectrum antibiotics)
  • Diagnosis: CT angiography
  • Embolus: embolectomy; peritonitis/infarcted bowel: laparotomy + resection
exam_pearl: "Initial" = fluids and heparin; "definitive" = embolectomy. Recent stroke excludes thrombolysis.

stem: Patient arrived to ER after head injury, upon Glasgow Coma Scale calculation, he can open eyes to painful stimuli, localizes the pain and says groaning sounds only, what is the calculated GCS for him?
why_right: Score each component: eyes open "to painful stimuli" = E2; "localizes the pain" = M5; "groaning sounds only" = incomprehensible sounds = V2. Total GCS = 2 + 5 + 2 = 9.
why_wrong_block:
A. 8 would require motor 4 (withdrawal from pain) instead of localizing, or one point less elsewhere; localizing to pain is motor 5.
C. 10 would need inappropriate words (V3) or eye opening to speech (E3); groaning is V2 and opening to pain is E2.
D. 11 overscores by two points, e.g. it would need both eyes to speech and words rather than sounds.
key_concept:
GCS = Eyes (4) + Verbal (5) + Motor (6), range 3 to 15.
  • Eyes: 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none
  • Verbal: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none
  • Motor: 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 withdraws, 3 abnormal flexion, 2 extension, 1 none
  • GCS ≤8: intubate
exam_pearl: Localizes (hand moves to the stimulus) = M5; withdraws (pulls away) = M4. Groaning = V2.

stem: Patient in 60s diagnosed with prostate cancer presenting with back pain, urine retention and maybe lower limb weakness. What is the Appropriate Next Step:
OptD: Oral analgesia and reassess after 24 hours
why_right: Prostate cancer most often metastasises to the spine, and "back pain, urine retention" with "lower limb weakness" means metastatic spinal cord compression, an oncological emergency. The next step is immediate high-dose IV dexamethasone to reduce cord edema, together with urgent whole-spine MRI and then radiotherapy or surgical decompression. Delay risks permanent paralysis and sphincter loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Physiotherapy is for mechanical back pain or rehabilitation after decompression; it delays treatment of a cord compression.
B. MRI is the right test but it must be urgent (same day), not outpatient; outpatient imaging is for back pain without red flags or neurological deficit.
D. Analgesia and reassessing after 24 hours wastes the window to save neurological function; that approach suits simple back pain without red flags.
key_concept:
Known cancer + back pain + neuro deficit/retention = cord compression until proven otherwise.
  • Common primaries: prostate, breast, lung
  • Step 1: high-dose IV dexamethasone
  • Step 2: urgent whole-spine MRI
  • Definitive: radiotherapy or surgical decompression
  • Late signs: urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, leg weakness
exam_pearl: "Outpatient MRI" is the trap: right test, wrong urgency.

stem: A mother was concerned of ADHD in her child (8 years). She described him at home as restless and cannot focus. Upon your assessment he is a calm child with normal behavior. What is the best action:
OptA: Obtain further information from parents and teachers
OptB: Start him on trial of amphetamines
OptC: Reassure the mother that these are normal behaviors at his age
why_right: ADHD diagnosis requires symptoms in at least two settings (home and school) that impair function. The mother reports symptoms at home, but the child is calm in the clinic, and office behavior is not reliable. The next step is to gather information from parents and teachers, usually with standardized rating scales, before diagnosing or treating.
why_wrong_block:
B. Start him on trial of amphetamines: stimulants are started only after the diagnosis is confirmed; a therapeutic trial is not a diagnostic test.
C. Reassure the mother that these are normal behaviors at his age: premature; dismissing her report without school information can miss true ADHD. Reassurance fits only after collateral history is normal.
D. Do neurological exam: part of a general assessment to exclude other causes, but it does not establish or refute ADHD, which is a clinical diagnosis based on history across settings.
key_concept:
ADHD is a clinical diagnosis:
  • Symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity for ≥6 months
  • Several symptoms present before age 12
  • Present in ≥2 settings (home, school)
  • Collect rating scales from parents AND teachers
  • Normal clinic behavior does not exclude ADHD
exam_pearl: A calm child in clinic does not rule out ADHD; get the teacher's report.

stem: 7-year-old child is reported to be hyperactive, restless, talks rapidly, and has violent outbursts. What intervention can help mitigate these issues?
OptB: Decreasing time spent on video games and watching television
why_right: A school age child who is "hyperactive, restless, talks rapidly" with "violent outbursts" fits ADHD with disruptive behavior. The lead-in asks what intervention helps mitigate these behaviors, and parent training in behavior management (rewarding positive behavior, planned ignoring, consistent limits and consequences) is the core non-drug intervention that reduces hyperactivity and aggression at home. It is the only option that directly targets the behavior itself.
why_wrong_block:
A. Preschool examinations are screening visits, not a treatment; this child is 7 and already of school age, so they do nothing to change his behavior.
B. Cutting screen time is reasonable general advice but has no proven effect as a treatment for ADHD symptoms or aggression; it would only be a supportive add on.
D. Special education resources are for a child with a learning disability or academic failure; nothing in the stem describes school performance problems, and they do not address outbursts at home.
key_concept:
ADHD behavior: parent training in behavior management is the first non-drug step.
  • Techniques: reward positive behavior, ignore minor disruptive behavior, time out, clear consistent rules
  • Preschool age: parent training is first line before medication
  • School age: stimulant medication plus behavioral therapy and school support
  • Toddler tantrums: reinforce positive behavior, no drugs
exam_pearl: When the stem asks for an intervention for a child's disruptive behavior, pick the option that trains the parents in behavior management, not a screening visit or general lifestyle advice.

stem: A healthy 7-year-old boy presents with short stature. He has normal growth velocity but delayed bone age. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Reassure the parents that the child will reach normal height by puberty
OptB: Order basic investigations (CBC, electrolytes, bone profile)
why_right: A healthy boy with normal growth velocity and delayed bone age has constitutional delay of growth and puberty. His growth is simply running late: puberty and the growth spurt come later than peers, and because the delayed bone age leaves more time to grow, he reaches a normal final height. Reassurance and follow-up of growth are the appropriate management.
why_wrong_block:
B. Screening bloods are chosen when growth velocity is slow, the child crosses centiles downward, or there are symptoms of systemic disease (malabsorption, renal, chronic illness). None are present here.
C. Sunlight is advice for vitamin D deficiency or rickets (bowed legs, widened wrists, bone pain), which is not suggested in a healthy child growing at a normal rate.
D. Avoiding dairy has no role; it would reduce calcium and protein intake. Dairy restriction is only for proven cow's milk protein allergy.
key_concept:
Short stature: normal velocity = normal variant; slow velocity = look for pathology.
  • Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, family history of late puberty, puberty late, normal final height
  • Familial short stature: bone age = chronological age, short parents, normal puberty, final height matches mid-parental target
  • Pathological (GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, chronic disease): falling velocity, often marked bone age delay
  • Turner syndrome in any short girl: karyotype
  • Mid-parental height best predicts final height
exam_pearl: Delayed bone age alone is not alarming; it is the growth velocity that tells you whether to investigate.

stem: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of cough followed by whooping sounds at the end of each episode. It is associated with perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no history of diarrhea. This illness has been preceded by runny nose a few days ago. History revealed he did not receive his 2-month vaccine yet. On examination, the child looks unwell and tachypneic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: paroxysmal episodes of cough followed by whooping sounds
why_right: Paroxysmal cough ending in a whoop, perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting, preceded by a catarrhal phase (runny nose), in an infant who missed his 2-month vaccine, is pertussis. There is no conjunctivitis and no diarrhea to suggest Chlamydia or adenovirus. Young unvaccinated infants are the group most at risk of severe disease.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adenovirus gives cough with fever, conjunctivitis and often diarrhea; choose it when those extra-respiratory features appear, which are absent here.
C. Mycoplasma pneumonia mainly affects school-age children and young adults, with a gradual dry cough and malaise; it is uncommon at 3 months and does not cause a whoop.
D. Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia has a staccato (not whooping) cough, preceding conjunctivitis, crackles, no fever and eosinophilia; the preceding illness here was a runny nose, not conjunctivitis.
key_concept:
Infant paroxysmal cough: the companion features decide.
  • Whoop + post-tussive vomiting, no conjunctivitis or diarrhea, unvaccinated: pertussis
  • Staccato cough + earlier conjunctivitis + crackles, no fever, eosinophilia: Chlamydia
  • Cough + conjunctivitis + fever + diarrhea: adenovirus
  • Pertussis: diagnose with nasopharyngeal PCR; treat patient and close contacts with a macrolide
  • Fever in pertussis suggests secondary pneumonia
exam_pearl: Missed vaccines + catarrhal start + whoop = pertussis; add conjunctivitis and diarrhea and it becomes adenovirus.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked A (MG).

stem: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of staccato cough, inspiration between each cough. It is associated with perioral cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no history of diarrhea. This illness has been preceded by conjunctivitis few days ago. On examination, the child looks unwell and tachypneic with auscultatory crackles. He has normal white blood cell count with elevated eosinophils on laboratory evaluation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The triad of a staccato cough, conjunctivitis a few days earlier and lower respiratory signs (tachypnea, crackles) in a young infant is Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia, acquired from the birth canal. The normal WBC with raised eosinophils is a classic supporting clue, and the absence of diarrhea argues against adenovirus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pertussis gives a whooping cough without conjunctivitis or crackles, usually after a runny nose rather than an eye infection; typical labs show lymphocytosis, not isolated eosinophilia.
B. Adenovirus also causes conjunctivitis and cough, but it brings fever and diarrhea; choose it when diarrhea is present.
C. Mycoplasma is a pneumonia of school-age children and adolescents and is not associated with neonatal conjunctivitis or eosinophilia.
key_concept:
Staccato cough + preceding conjunctivitis + afebrile pneumonia in an infant under 3 months = Chlamydia trachomatis.
  • Conjunctivitis typically appears around 2 weeks, pneumonia at about 4 to 12 weeks
  • Labs: normal WBC with eosinophilia
  • CXR: bilateral interstitial infiltrates with hyperinflation
  • Treatment: oral macrolide (azithromycin or erythromycin)
  • Diarrhea present = adenovirus; whoop alone = pertussis
exam_pearl: Staccato cough with eosinophilia and a history of sticky eyes is Chlamydia, even if the paroxysms cause cyanosis and vomiting like pertussis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked D (MG).

stem: A 3-month-old boy presented to the Emergency Room with history paroxysmal episodes of cough associated with an inspiratory whoop and possessive emesis. It is associated with fever, conjunctival redness and diarrhea. His immunization is up to date. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Although the cough has an inspiratory whoop with post-tussive emesis, the accompanying fever, conjunctival redness and diarrhea point to a multisystem viral infection: adenovirus. The infant is also fully immunized, which makes pertussis less likely. Diarrhea is the key feature separating adenovirus from Chlamydia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pertussis causes isolated whooping paroxysms without fever, conjunctivitis or diarrhea, typically in an unvaccinated infant; a whoop alone is not enough when these extra features are present.
C. Mycoplasma pneumonia is a disease of older children and young adults and does not cause conjunctivitis with diarrhea in a 3-month-old.
D. Chlamydia also follows conjunctivitis, but it is afebrile, has a staccato cough and does not cause diarrhea.
key_concept:
Conjunctivitis + cough: check for fever and diarrhea.
  • Fever + diarrhea + conjunctivitis + cough: adenovirus (supportive care)
  • No fever, no diarrhea, staccato cough, eosinophilia: Chlamydia (macrolide)
  • Isolated whoop, no eye or gut signs, unvaccinated: pertussis (macrolide)
  • Adenovirus can also cause pharyngitis, gastroenteritis, croup, cystitis and pneumonia
exam_pearl: A whoop does not automatically mean pertussis; conjunctivitis plus diarrhea in a vaccinated infant means adenovirus.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked B (MG).

stem: A 71 years old man known IHD, complaining of severe central abdominal pain for 10 hours, and vomit 3 times; on examination there was mild tenderness, there mild bowl sluggish. Amylase 400 and WBC 22K.
why_right: An elderly man with "IHD" (cardiovascular embolic/thrombotic risk) has "severe" central abdominal pain but only "mild tenderness": pain out of proportion to examination, the hallmark of acute mesenteric ischemia. Marked leukocytosis ("WBC 22K") reflects bowel ischemia, and sluggish bowel sounds suggest evolving ileus. Amylase is often moderately raised in bowel ischemia, so it does not make this pancreatitis.
why_wrong_block: B. Acute pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back with clear epigastric tenderness and a risk factor such as gallstones or alcohol; it is chosen when amylase/lipase is ≥3 times the upper limit with characteristic pain. Here the cardiac history and pain out of proportion favour ischemia.
key_concept:
Old + cardiac disease + severe pain, soft abdomen = mesenteric ischemia.
  • Leukocytosis and lactic acidosis support ischemia
  • Amylase can rise in ischemic bowel: not specific for pancreatitis
  • Pancreatitis = 2 of 3: typical pain, enzymes ≥3x ULN, imaging
  • Confirm ischemia with CT angiography
exam_pearl: A raised amylase does not equal pancreatitis; the cardiac patient with pain out of proportion is ischemia.

stem: 5 year old child going for preschool vaccination, what is the most important prevaccination preassessment
why_right: The preschool booster at 5 years includes live vaccines such as MMR and varicella. Antibodies from a recent immunoglobulin or other antibody-containing blood product can neutralise these live viruses, so the dose may fail and must be deferred for a set interval. That is why this history is the key pre-vaccination check in this recall; inactivated vaccines are not affected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR or other routine childhood vaccines; it matters mainly for yellow fever vaccine, and current guidance gives influenza vaccine to egg-allergic children without special precautions.
C. Mild illness with or without fever is not a contraindication; only moderate to severe acute illness is a precaution that delays vaccination, so a fever check alone is less decisive.
D. Inspecting the previous vaccine site has no bearing on whether the next dose is safe or effective; a past mild local reaction is not a contraindication.
key_concept:
Pre-vaccination screening: true contraindications vs misconceptions.
  • Contraindication: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or a vaccine component
  • Live vaccines: avoid in significant immunosuppression and pregnancy; defer after immunoglobulin or blood products
  • Transfusion delays live vaccines only; inactivated vaccines are given on schedule
  • Precaution: moderate or severe acute illness
  • Not contraindications: mild illness, antibiotics, penicillin allergy, family history of vaccine reactions
exam_pearl: Recent immunoglobulin matters for live vaccines (MMR, varicella), not for killed ones; that is why it dominates the 5-year booster check.

stem: 46-year-old woman undergoes a routine screening mammogram, reported as completely normal. She has no symptoms and no family history. When should she do her next mammogram?
highlight_terms_source: screening mammogram, reported as completely normal
why_right: This recall's key is annual screening because she is "46" with a normal mammogram, no symptoms and no family history, i.e. average risk in the 40 to 50 age band, where the taught schedule is yearly mammography. From 50 to 74 the interval lengthens to every 2 years, which is why the same scenario in a woman above 50 is keyed to 2 years.
why_wrong_block:
A. 6 months is a short-interval follow-up for a probably benign finding (BI-RADS 3), not for a completely normal screening mammogram.
C. 2 years is the interval taught for average-risk women aged 50 to 74 (and some guidelines apply it from 40); in this card's 40 to 50 rule the answer is yearly.
D. 3 years is not a mammography interval; it is the Pap smear (cytology) interval for cervical screening.
key_concept:
Mammography interval by age (average risk).
  • 40 to 50: yearly (this card's rule)
  • 50 to 74: every 2 years
  • BI-RADS 3: short-interval follow-up at 6 months
  • Pap cytology: every 3 years (do not confuse)
exam_pearl: Age decides it: under 50 yearly, 50 and above every 2 years.
compiler_note: Compiler note: "Above 50 → C. 2 years"

stem: A mechanic had an accidental injection of oil dissolving in his index finger. The finger is red and swollen with mild tenderness and normal joint movement. What to give??
why_right: An accidental injection of oil/solvent into the finger is a high-pressure injection injury, a surgical emergency even when the finger looks benign ("mild tenderness and normal joint movement"). The injected material tracks along tendon sheaths and fascial planes, causing chemical inflammation, ischemia and necrosis, so the finger needs urgent surgical exploration, decompression and debridement (drainage) of the foreign material. Delay greatly increases the risk of amputation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics alone do not remove the injected material; they are an adjunct given alongside surgery. Antibiotics alone fit simple cellulitis without a retained injected substance.
B. Antibiotics and steroids are sometimes used as adjuncts after surgical debridement, but neither removes the oil, so they cannot replace surgery.
D. Elevation and ice is for a minor soft tissue contusion or sprain; it gives false reassurance and lets necrosis progress in an injection injury.
key_concept:
High-pressure injection injury (paint, grease, oil, solvent) = emergency surgical debridement.
  • Typical: worker with grease or paint gun, index finger of the non-dominant hand
  • Small entry wound, deceptively mild early exam
  • Organic solvents/paint are more destructive than grease
  • Treatment: urgent exploration, decompression, debridement + antibiotics
  • Delay → amputation
exam_pearl: A tiny wound and a normal-looking finger are the trap: injection injury always goes to theatre.

stem: 79-year-old male patient, post cholecystectomy, developed confusion and agitation. What to do?
why_right: An elderly patient who becomes acutely "confused and agitated" after surgery has postoperative delirium. First line management is to treat the cause and use non-pharmacological measures, of which reorientation (clock, calendar, familiar faces, glasses and hearing aids, explaining where they are) is the key step. Drugs and restraints are reserved for when these fail and the patient is a danger to self or others.
why_wrong_block:
A. Physical restraint worsens agitation, prolongs delirium and causes injury; it is a last resort only for immediate danger when other measures fail.
B. A quiet room alone is part of the environmental care but isolation without orientation cues can worsen confusion; orientation is the active intervention asked for.
C. Antipsychotics (e.g. low dose haloperidol) are used only when non-drug measures fail and agitation is severe or dangerous; they are not the first step in an elderly patient.
key_concept:
Delirium management ladder: find and treat the cause, then non-drug measures, then drugs only if dangerous.
  • Search for cause: infection, hypoxia, electrolytes, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics), urinary retention, pain
  • Non-drug: reorientation, family presence, glasses and hearing aids, sleep and day/night cues, early mobilization
  • Severe agitation with risk of harm: low dose antipsychotic
  • Avoid benzodiazepines (except alcohol withdrawal) and physical restraints
exam_pearl: In delirium questions, "give antipsychotic" and "restrain" are traps when the patient is not yet a danger; orientation and non-drug measures come first.

stem: 4 months old with poor weight gain. At birth it was 3.3 kg, then became 4 kg. His mother uses 2 spoons of milk in 90 mL water, she feeds him every 3 hours. She's 19 years old, that's her first baby. What is the most likely cause of failure to thrive?
highlight_terms_source: 2 spoons of milk in 90 mL water
19 years old, that's her first baby
why_right: The infant has gained only 0.7 kg in 4 months (3.3 to 4 kg), far below the expected gain of roughly 25 to 30 g/day in early infancy. Feeding every 3 hours is an adequate frequency, so the problem is what is in the bottle: 2 spoons in 90 mL is over-diluted: most powdered formulas use 1 level scoop per 30 mL, so 90 mL needs 3 scoops, and each feed is short of calories. A young, first-time mother points to an error of inexperience in preparing formula.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neglect requires evidence such as missed feeds, poor hygiene, unexplained injuries or a disengaged caregiver; here the mother feeds regularly and the error is technical.
B. Celiac disease needs gluten exposure, which starts with weaning to cereals after about 6 months; it presents later with diarrhea, distension and buttock wasting, not in an exclusively formula-fed 4-month-old.
D. Feeding every 3 hours (about 8 feeds a day) is normal for this age, so frequency is not the problem.
key_concept:
Failure to thrive in an infant: start with the feeding history (volume, frequency, preparation).
  • Expected gain: about 25 to 30 g/day for 0 to 3 months, about 20 g/day for 3 to 6 months
  • Birth weight doubles by 5 months and triples by 1 year
  • Formula must be made with the scoop and water ratio on the tin; over-dilution gives poor gain, over-concentration risks hypernatremia
  • Downward crossing of centiles needs evaluation
  • Most infant FTT is non-organic (inadequate intake)
exam_pearl: Before suspecting disease or neglect, ask exactly how the formula is mixed; a wrong scoop count is the commonest fixable cause.

stem: A man presents with small papules on his face after shaving. (No pain, tenderness, erythema, or purulent discharge was mentioned.) What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small papules on his face after shaving
key_concept:
Size and depth decide: superficial follicular papules or pustules = folliculitis; deep tender nodule = furuncle; several merged furuncles = carbuncle.
  • Folliculitis: small perifollicular papules or pustules, sites of shaving, sweat and abrasion
  • Furuncle (boil): tender nodule around one follicle, drain if fluctuant
  • Carbuncle: several adjacent follicles, plaque with multiple pus points, classically the nape of the neck
  • Pseudofolliculitis barbae: ingrown beard hairs after close shaving, small papules in the beard area
exam_pearl: Many small follicular papules = folliculitis; one big painful nodule = furuncle.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Child diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome came to ER with abdominal pain and distention; mother said he vomit immediately everything he take. What could be?
why_right: A child with known nephrotic syndrome who develops abdominal pain, distension and vomiting has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proven otherwise. Urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement plus ascitic fluid make these children prone to peritonitis, classically pneumococcal. The same scenario is keyed to peritonitis, the complication these children are at higher risk of.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pancreatitis: causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting, but nephrotic syndrome itself does not specifically predispose to it; consider it only if lipase is raised or the child is on drugs that cause it.
B. Hepatitis: presents with jaundice, RUQ tenderness and raised transaminases; nephrotic syndrome does not increase hepatitis risk and it would not explain acute distension with persistent vomiting.
D. Heart failure: gives edema, hepatomegaly and tachycardia with breathlessness, not an acute painful distended abdomen; the edema here is explained by hypoalbuminemia.
key_concept:
Nephrotic syndrome complications = infection + thrombosis.
  • Infection: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae), cellulitis
  • Cause: urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement, ascites as a culture medium
  • Thrombosis: hypercoagulable state (antithrombin III loss), renal vein thrombosis
  • Clue for SBP: abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, fever, rebound tenderness
exam_pearl: Nephrotic child + new abdominal pain and distension = think peritonitis first, not gastritis or hepatitis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No typed answer; an embedded screenshot of the same question marks **C. Peritonitis: 'A 5-year-old boy who is known to have nephrotic syndrome presents to the clinic with severe abdominal pain and distention. He has omitted once a clear stomach content of his last meal. No diarrhea or constipation. Which of the following this patient is at higher risk to have? A. Hepatitis B. Gastritis C. Peritonitis D. Appendicitis'.

stem: Developed large neck swelling on the left side. On exam it is large 10 cm in size, US FNA showed clear lymphatic fluid. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A large lateral (left) neck swelling in a young child with "clear lymphatic fluid" on aspiration is a cystic hygroma (macrocystic lymphatic malformation). It is benign, so the aim is removal or ablation of the malformation; of the listed options only surgery treats it, and excision is the definitive option for a large 10 cm lesion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation is not appropriate for a large 10 cm lesion, which risks airway compression, infection and hemorrhage into the cyst; spontaneous regression is uncommon.
C. Chemotherapy is for malignancy (e.g. lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma); clear lymphatic fluid indicates a benign malformation.
D. Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.
key_concept:
Pediatric neck masses:
  • Midline, moves with tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst, excision (Sistrunk)
  • Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid: branchial cyst, excision
  • Lateral / posterior triangle, soft, transilluminates, clear lymph fluid: cystic hygroma, sclerotherapy then surgery
  • Hard, fixed, systemic symptoms: think malignancy, biopsy
exam_pearl: Clear lymphatic fluid in a lateral neck mass = cystic hygroma; if sclerotherapy is offered, it is usually first for macrocystic lesions.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No Sclerotherapy (among the options).

stem: 12-week-old child with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome with the mother concerned about increased risk for liver lesion. What tumor marker will you use?
OptD: Urine Homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)
why_right: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome carries an increased risk of embryonal tumours, and the liver lesion the mother worries about is hepatoblastoma. Serum AFP is the tumour marker for hepatoblastoma and is used, together with abdominal ultrasound, to screen these infants in early childhood.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine oxalic level: used to look for hyperoxaluria in recurrent kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis, not a tumour marker.
C. PSA: a marker of prostate disease in adult men; it has no role in a 12-week-old infant or in liver tumours.
D. Urine HVA and VMA: catecholamine metabolites used for neuroblastoma (adrenal or paraspinal mass), not for a liver lesion.
key_concept:
Match the paediatric tumour to its marker.
  • Hepatoblastoma: AFP
  • Neuroblastoma: urine HVA and VMA
  • BWS screening: abdominal ultrasound (Wilms, hepatoblastoma) plus serum AFP (hepatoblastoma)
  • Wilms tumour: no blood marker; imaging
  • Interpret infant AFP against age norms, as it is physiologically high early in life
exam_pearl: BWS + liver = hepatoblastoma = AFP; BWS + kidney = Wilms = ultrasound.
compiler_note: Compiler note: AFP is used to screen for hepatoblastoma in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

stem: Patient came to ER after he loss concious; after he regained it he experience sever headache describing it as worse headache he ever had. Plain CT showed: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Hydrocephalus. How are you going to investigate the affected artery?
why_right: The diagnosis is already made: "worst headache ever" after collapse, and plain CT shows SAH with hydrocephalus. The question now is "investigate the affected artery", i.e. find the bleeding aneurysm or vascular anomaly. Once CT confirms SAH, the next step is CT angiography, which is fast, noninvasive and shows the aneurysm to plan coiling or clipping.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI with contrast is slower, harder in a sick patient with hydrocephalus and less sensitive for acute blood; MR angiography is an alternative mainly when CT contrast is not possible, not the standard first vessel study.
B. Lumbar puncture only confirms SAH (xanthochromia, persistent RBCs) when CT is negative and more than 6 hours from onset; here CT is already positive and LP gives no information about the artery.
D. Transcranial Doppler is used after SAH to monitor for vasospasm, not to locate the ruptured aneurysm.
key_concept:
Thunderclap headache workup: confirm the bleed, then image the vessels.
  • Step 1: noncontrast CT head
  • CT positive for SAH: CT angiography to define the aneurysm
  • CT negative within 6 h of onset: SAH ruled out, look for other causes
  • CT negative after 6 h: lumbar puncture (xanthochromia, RBCs not clearing tube 1 to 4)
  • Abnormal LP: CT angiography
  • Digital subtraction angiography: gold standard if CTA is negative or for intervention
exam_pearl: "Diagnose SAH" with negative late CT = LP; "find the artery" after positive CT = CT angiography.

stem: RTA with dull percussion on exam and chest tube was inserted, Which of the following is an indication for surgical intervention?
why_right: Dull percussion after an RTA means hemothorax, and the chest tube both treats it and measures the bleeding. Thoracotomy is indicated when the tube shows major bleeding: a large initial output or continued drainage of about 200 ml/hr over several hours. Of the listed options only the ongoing 200 ml/hr output matches a recognised criterion.
why_wrong_block:
A. 500 ml initially is far below the threshold; the immediate output that mandates thoracotomy is more than 1500 ml.
C. Hemopneumothorax is managed with the same chest tube; the presence of air plus blood is not itself an indication for surgery.
D. Some drop in Hb and hematocrit is expected with any hemothorax and resuscitation; the trigger is chest tube output or hemodynamic decompensation, not a lab change alone.
key_concept:
Hemothorax: chest tube first, thoracotomy if the tube shows major bleeding.
  • Initial output more than 1500 ml
  • Ongoing output 200 to 300 ml/hr for several (classically 4) hours
  • Decompensation after initial stabilisation
  • Unstable patient: decision is by tube output, not CT
exam_pearl: The immediate threshold is 1500 ml, not 500 ml; smaller numbers are distractors.

stem: MVA patient with hemothorax managed by thoracostomy (chest tube). What's the indication of thoracotomy?
why_right: After a chest tube for traumatic hemothorax, thoracotomy is indicated by the volume and rate of bleeding. Persistent drainage of about 200 ml/hr for 4 hours means ongoing bleeding that the tube cannot control, so it is a classic criterion for thoracotomy.
why_wrong_block: B. An initial 500 ml is a moderate hemothorax that the chest tube alone usually manages; the immediate criterion is more than 1500 ml.
key_concept:
Indications for thoracotomy after chest tube in hemothorax:
  • Initial drainage more than 1500 ml
  • 200 to 300 ml/hr for 4 hours
  • Hemodynamic decompensation after initial stabilisation
exam_pearl: Two routes to thoracotomy: one big dump (more than 1500 ml) or a steady leak (200 ml/hr for 4 h).

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents to the Paediatric Emergency Department in the early morning hours with a barking cough, that worsens with crying. There is a history of mild cough and temperatures around 38° C (rectal) over the last 3 days. Physical examination confirms an inflamed throat and mild suprasternal retractions. Blood pressure 95/65 mmHg, Heart rate 90 /min, Respiratory rate 34 /min, Temperature 39.3° C. Which of the following is the most likely at auscultatory finding?
highlight_terms_source: barking cough, that worsens with crying
why_right: A 3-year-old with a barking cough that worsens with crying, a few days of mild cough and fever, and suprasternal retractions has croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). The subglottic narrowing produces inspiratory stridor, which is the expected finding; the lung fields themselves are usually clear.
why_wrong_block:
A. Crepitation: crackles come from alveolar or small airway fluid, as in pneumonia or bronchiolitis; croup is an upper airway disease.
B. Wheezing: an expiratory sound of lower airway narrowing (asthma, bronchiolitis), not the inspiratory upper airway noise of croup.
D. Gasp: gasping is an agonal pattern of impending arrest, not the typical finding in a child with mild retractions and stable vitals.
key_concept:
Where the noise comes from tells you the level of obstruction.
  • Upper airway (croup, epiglottitis, foreign body in larynx): inspiratory stridor
  • Lower airway (asthma, bronchiolitis): expiratory wheeze
  • Alveoli (pneumonia): crackles
  • Croup: parainfluenza, barking cough, worse at night and with crying
  • Croup is a clinical diagnosis; treat with steroids, add nebulized epinephrine if distress
exam_pearl: Barking cough = croup = stridor; if the child drools and looks toxic, think epiglottitis instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed version: 'kid have cough worsening with crying he ask what will you hear in auscultation' with options A. Strider, B. Weezing, C. Crackles, D. Gasping (no answer marked). Answer taken from the screenshot on the next page, where C. Stridor is marked with **.

stem: A 6-year-old boy complains of passing Coca-cola-coloured urine for the last week, with periorbital puffiness worse in the morning and fever. Congested throat and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy on exam. Which is the next best investigation?
why_right: Cola-coloured urine, periorbital puffiness worse in the morning and a recent congested throat with cervical lymphadenopathy point to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The first investigation is urinalysis, which confirms hematuria, RBC casts and proteinuria and so establishes a nephritic picture before further tests.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine culture: right when dysuria, frequency or a febrile child without another focus suggest UTI; here the fever fits the throat infection and the dark urine is glomerular hematuria, not infection.
B. Renal ultrasound: helpful for stones, obstruction or structural anomalies, but adds little in suspected acute glomerulonephritis.
C. Renal biopsy: reserved for atypical or non-resolving cases (persistent low C3, rapidly rising creatinine, nephrotic-range proteinuria), never the first step.
key_concept:
Suspected PSGN workup ladder.
  • 1st: urinalysis (hematuria, RBC casts, protein)
  • Then: serum creatinine for renal function
  • Best supporting test: low C3 with normal C4
  • Evidence of strep: ASO or anti-DNase B
  • Timing: about 1 to 2 weeks after pharyngitis, 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo
  • Management: supportive (fluid and salt restriction, treat hypertension)
exam_pearl: If the stem already shows RBCs in urine, the next test moves on to creatinine or C3, not urinalysis.

stem: A kid who won't move his lower limb presents with a swollen, hot, tender knee. What to do?
why_right: A child who won't move his lower limb with a swollen, hot, tender knee has septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Synovial fluid aspiration (cell count, Gram stain, culture) is the key step because it confirms the diagnosis and identifies the organism, and it should ideally be done before antibiotics are started.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood culture: a useful adjunct, but it is positive in only a minority and cannot confirm joint infection on its own.
C. IV antibiotics: essential and given promptly, right after joint fluid is obtained; giving them first can sterilise the aspirate and hide the organism. Right first only if aspiration would be delayed in an unstable or septic child.
key_concept:
Suspected septic arthritis: tap, then treat.
  • Clues: fever, refusal to move or bear weight, hot swollen joint, pain on passive movement
  • Key test: joint aspiration (synovial WBC very high, neutrophil predominant, Gram stain, culture)
  • Commonest organism: Staphylococcus aureus
  • Then: empirical IV antibiotics and surgical washout or drainage
  • X-ray is often normal early
exam_pearl: Asked for the most important test or what to do first: aspirate the joint; asked for treatment after the tap: IV antibiotics.

stem: A 7-year-old child presents with signs of meningitis. Laboratory investigations reveal a blood glucose level of 4.8 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows: Protein: 450 mg/dL (normal range: 150–450), Glucose: 3.8 mg/dL (normal range: 2.8–4.8), Predominant lymphocytic pleocytosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of meningitis in this case?
why_right: The CSF shows a normal glucose (3.8, within its normal range and close to the blood level of 4.8), protein within the normal range, and a lymphocytic pleocytosis. Normal glucose plus normal protein plus lymphocytes is the viral meningitis pattern. The units in the recall are garbled, so read each value against the normal range given.
why_wrong_block:
B. Bacterial: gives a low CSF glucose, raised protein and neutrophil predominance with turbid fluid.
C. Tuberculous: also lymphocytic, but with low glucose and markedly raised protein, usually after weeks of fever and headache in an endemic setting.
key_concept:
Read CSF by glucose first, then cell type.
  • Bacterial: low glucose, high protein, neutrophils
  • Viral: normal glucose, normal or mildly raised protein, lymphocytes
  • TB: low glucose, high protein, lymphocytes
  • Fungal: similar to TB; think immunocompromise
exam_pearl: Lymphocytes alone do not mean viral: a low glucose with lymphocytes means TB.

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents to the clinic for an annual physical assessment. The patient has normal growth and development and is able to do usual activities. His elder brother died due to a sudden cardiac death while walking to work. On physical examination, there is no cardiac murmur. Pulses are equal in all extremities. Which condition must be excluded before any sport is allowed?
highlight_terms_source: elder brother died due to a sudden cardiac death
why_right: An elder brother with sudden cardiac death in a young, otherwise well boy raises suspicion of an inherited cause, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young people. It is autosomal dominant and is often silent at rest, so a normal exam with no murmur does not exclude it; ECG and echocardiography are needed before sports clearance.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bicuspid aortic valve: usually gives an ejection click or murmur and is not a typical familial cause of sudden death in youth.
B. Patent ductus arteriosus: produces a continuous machinery murmur (absent here) and is not a hereditary cause of sudden cardiac death.
C. Ventricular septal defect: produces a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border (absent here) and does not cause familial sudden death.
key_concept:
Family history of young sudden cardiac death: screen first-degree relatives.
  • HCM: autosomal dominant sarcomere disease, leading cause of SCD in young athletes
  • Murmur, if present, increases with Valsalva and standing
  • Screening: ECG and echocardiography
  • Others to consider: long QT, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronary artery
exam_pearl: No murmur does not clear HCM; the obstruction murmur may appear only with Valsalva or exercise.

stem: Treatment of chalazion:
why_right: A chalazion is a sterile, painless granulomatous lump from a blocked meibomian gland, not an infection. First-line treatment is warm compresses with lid massage several times a day, and most resolve within weeks to months.
why_wrong_block: A. Antibiotics do not help a sterile granuloma; they are reserved for a secondarily infected lesion or associated preseptal cellulitis.
key_concept:
Chalazion = painless, sterile, meibomian gland lump; hordeolum (stye) = painful acute infection.
  • Chalazion first line: warm compress and lid massage
  • Persistent chalazion: incision and curettage or intralesional steroid
  • Recurrent chalazion in the same site in an older adult: biopsy to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma
  • Stye: also warm compress; antibiotics only if spreading infection
exam_pearl: Recurrent chalazion at the same spot in an elderly patient = biopsy, not more compresses.

stem: After accident a patient came with warm lower extremities with normal chest exam , BP was low, HR70 what kind of shock?
why_right: Trauma with low BP but HR 70 (no reflex tachycardia) and warm lower extremities points to neurogenic shock. Spinal cord injury cuts sympathetic outflow, causing vasodilation (warm skin) and unopposed vagal tone (normal or slow pulse). The normal chest exam also argues against tension pneumothorax or tamponade.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypovolemic shock causes vasoconstriction with cold, clammy extremities and tachycardia; it would be the answer if the patient were cold and tachycardic after trauma.
C. Cardiogenic or obstructive shock gives cold peripheries, tachycardia and cardiac signs such as raised JVP or muffled heart sounds, none of which are present.
D. Septic shock is also warm, but needs an infective source and produces tachycardia; it does not appear immediately after an accident.
key_concept:
Shock type by skin temperature and heart rate:
  • Cold + tachycardia: hypovolemic or cardiogenic
  • Warm + tachycardia: septic
  • Warm + normal or slow HR after trauma: neurogenic
  • Only cardiogenic has raised PCWP; only septic has raised cardiac output
exam_pearl: Hypotension without tachycardia after trauma = think spinal cord (neurogenic), but still exclude bleeding.

stem: A newborn develops respiratory distress shortly after birth. Chest X-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures. What is the most important in management?
why_right: Respiratory distress shortly after birth with fluid in the interlobar fissures on chest X-ray is transient tachypnea of the newborn, caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid and usually self-resolving. This recall's key is giving fluids, reasoning that a tachypneic newborn who cannot feed safely needs IV fluid support while the condition settles.
why_wrong_block:
A. NPO: withholding oral feeds while the baby is tachypneic reduces aspiration risk, but on its own it does not maintain hydration; this recall keys fluid support as the most important step.
B. Empirical antibiotics: right when sepsis or congenital pneumonia is suspected (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, worsening course); TTN itself is not infective.
key_concept:
TTN vs RDS in the newborn.
  • TTN: term, often C-section, fluid in fissures and perihilar streaks, resolves in 1 to 3 days
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground glass (reticulogranular) X-ray
  • TTN care: supportive oxygen or CPAP, monitor, withhold oral feeds if tachypneic, IV fluids
  • RDS care: CPAP and surfactant, antenatal steroids for prevention
exam_pearl: Fissure fluid in a term C-section baby = TTN = supportive care, not surfactant or antibiotics.

stem: A female patient presents with decreased need for sleep, increased energy, and rapid speech. What is the most appropriate treatment? No Any Other Feature Mentioned In The Recall , Just Acute Mania (No Obesity , DLP , HTN , Etc Not “Mentioned” )
highlight_terms_source: decreased need for sleep, increased energy, and rapid speech
key_concept:
Acute mania: lithium, valproate or a second generation antipsychotic are all first line options; stop any antidepressant.
  • Severe agitation or psychosis: antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone) for fast control
  • Classic euphoric mania and maintenance: lithium
  • Mixed features or rapid cycling: valproate often preferred
  • Pregnancy: avoid valproate
  • Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder is contraindicated
exam_pearl: Decide with the lead-in words: "rapid control" or agitation points to an antipsychotic, "mood stabilizer" or maintenance points to lithium, and an SSRI is never the answer in mania.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Anal fissure 7, 3 (o'clock) management?
key_concept:
Fissure site matters.
  • 6 o'clock (posterior midline): typical, most common
  • 12 o'clock (anterior midline): typical, more common in women (postpartum)
  • Lateral (e.g. 3 or 7 o'clock), multiple or painless: atypical; think Crohn's, TB, HIV, syphilis, carcinoma; examine under anaesthesia with biopsy
  • 3, 7, 11 o'clock are the classic positions of internal haemorrhoids, a common recall mix-up
  • Acute: topical cream; chronic failing medical therapy: sphincterotomy

stem: Hepatitis serology: Positive HBsAg, Negative HBsAb, Positive HBcAb IgG, Negative HBcAb IgM, Positive HBeAg. What's management?
key_concept:
Read HBV serology marker by marker.
  • HBsAg+: current infection (acute or chronic)
  • IgM anti-HBc+: acute; IgG anti-HBc+ with HBsAg+: chronic
  • Anti-HBs+ alone: vaccinated; anti-HBs+ with anti-HBc+: recovered
  • HBeAg+: high replication and infectivity; anti-HBe+: lower infectivity
  • Chronic HBV work-up: HBV DNA, ALT, liver fibrosis assessment; treat with tenofovir or entecavir if criteria met
  • Exposed non-immune person or newborn of carrier mother: HBIG + vaccine
exam_pearl: HBIG is prophylaxis for the exposed person (or the baby), never treatment for the person who already carries HBsAg.

stem: A 40 YO male who had "A" relative (didn't determine degree of relative) diagnosed with colon cancer at age of 50 is concerned about colon cancer screening.
key_concept:
Family history changes the start age, and sometimes the interval.
  • Average risk: start at 45 (choose 50 if 45 is not offered), colonoscopy every 10 years
  • First-degree relative with CRC before 60 (or two first-degree relatives): colonoscopy at 40 or 10 years before the youngest diagnosis, every 5 years
  • Second-degree relative only: treat as average risk
  • Other average-risk tools: flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography every 5 years, FOBT yearly
exam_pearl: "Relative" without a degree is the trap: first-degree moves screening to 40; second-degree leaves the patient at average risk.

stem: A 7-year-old patient presents with abnormal jerky movements, sore throat, and fever. His brother and sister had similar symptoms with fever. What is the most appropriate action?
OptA: Treat fever and reassure the parents
OptC: Perform throat culture and start penicillin
OptD: Obtain brain imaging and lumbar puncture
key_concept:
Fever plus abnormal movements in a child: first separate benign rigors from CNS infection and from post-streptococcal disease.
  • Rigors: conscious, stops with antipyretic, normal neuro exam
  • Meningitis or sepsis: neck stiffness, drowsiness, rash; give IV antibiotics
  • Encephalitis: seizures, confusion, focal signs; imaging and LP
  • Sydenham chorea: weeks after strep throat, irregular purposeless movements, emotional lability
  • GAS pharyngitis: confirm by rapid test or throat culture before antibiotics
exam_pearl: Sydenham chorea appears weeks after the sore throat, often without fever; chorea during an acute febrile sore throat should prompt you to rule out CNS infection.

stem: There was patient with clinical scenario of Alzheimer's prescribed donepezil but no improvement was noticed (literally said no improvement, not little, not incomplete) for 6 months. His MMSE was 19 and now is 12. Asking how to adjust his meds:
why_right: This recall's key is to switch donepezil to memantine because the patient had "no improvement" at all on an adequate trial (6 months) while MMSE fell from 19 to 12, now in the moderate range. Treating him as a non-responder, the reasoning is to change drug class to the NMDA antagonist memantine, which is licensed for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, rather than persist with or add to a drug that has failed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sertraline treats depression or anxiety in dementia; there is no mention of mood symptoms and it does not slow cognitive decline.
B. Adding memantine to donepezil is used in moderate to severe disease when the patient is benefiting from or tolerating the cholinesterase inhibitor; the stem stresses complete lack of response, which the key treats as a reason to switch rather than combine.
D. Rivastigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor with the same mechanism; switching within the class is mainly for intolerance of donepezil rather than lack of effect, and the decline is now moderate.
key_concept:
Alzheimer drug ladder by severity:
  • Mild to moderate: cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine)
  • Moderate with intolerance or contraindication to cholinesterase inhibitors: memantine
  • Severe: memantine
  • Moderate to severe already on a cholinesterase inhibitor: memantine can be added
  • Rough MMSE bands: mild 21 to 26, moderate 10 to 20, severe below 10
exam_pearl: The stem's emphasis on "no improvement" drives the switch to a different class; with partial benefit the expected move is to add memantine.

stem: Child came to ER before 12 hours with fever and SOB, yesterday he had sore throat and dysphagia. On exam he looks toxic, immobile in a chair, opens his mouth with drooling of saliva, tachycardic, tachypneic and fever 40. Oxygen sat 88%. What's the next step?
highlight_terms_source: immobile in a chair, opens his mouth with drooling of saliva
key_concept:
Epiglottitis = airway first, then sepsis workup and antibiotics.
  • Picture: high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod or immobile, muffled voice, no barking cough.
  • Clinical diagnosis: do not examine the throat or upset the child.
  • Secure airway in a controlled setting (ICU or OR) by the most skilled operator.
  • Then blood culture plus IV 3rd generation cephalosporin.
  • Croup: barking cough, stridor, well looking; treat with steroids plus nebulized epinephrine.
exam_pearl: Drooling plus toxic look plus no barking cough means epiglottitis, so the answer is about securing the airway, never steroids or the ward.

stem: Child with difficulty swallowing and congested throat, febrile, no cough, she is ill and sitting silently in her mother's lap but with her neck extended?
key_concept:
Epiglottitis sequence: keep the child calm, secure the airway, then culture and antibiotics.
  • Clues: toxic, drooling, dysphagia, no cough, tripod or sniffing (neck extended) posture.

  • Step 2: blood culture plus IV 3rd generation cephalosporin.
  • Croup instead: barking cough, stridor, nontoxic; steroids plus nebulized epinephrine.

stem: 5-year-old child presents to the Emergency Room with severe sore throat, high fever and increasing difficulty breathing over 8 hours. On examination, ill toxic looking child with drooling of saliva and sitting immobile with open mouth. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, heart rate 115/min, respiratory rate 32/min, temperature 38.8 °C, oxygen saturation 95%. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action should be taken?
OptA: Urgent referral to ENT for tonsillectomy
OptB: Complete sepsis work up, followed by antibiotics for 7 days
OptC: Send home on oral antibiotics for 7 days and referral to ENT
OptD: Urgent admission to ICU for intubation then sepsis work to follow
highlight_terms_source: ill toxic looking child with drooling of saliva
why_right: Severe sore throat, high fever and difficulty breathing developing over 8 hours in a toxic child who is drooling and sitting immobile with open mouth is acute epiglottitis. The lead in is the immediate action: the risk is sudden complete airway closure, so the airway is secured first (ICU admission for intubation) and the sepsis workup and antibiotics follow. The normal saturation (95%) does not make the airway safe.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urgent referral to ENT for tonsillectomy: tonsillectomy is elective treatment for recurrent tonsillitis or obstructive sleep apnea, not an emergency airway measure.
B. Complete sepsis work up, followed by antibiotics for 7 days: cultures and antibiotics are needed, but only after the airway is secured; doing them first can provoke obstruction.
C. Send home on oral antibiotics for 7 days and referral to ENT: suits a well child with simple bacterial pharyngitis; a toxic, drooling child must never be discharged.
key_concept:
Epiglottitis: airway first, then sepsis workup and IV antibiotics.
  • Picture: rapid onset over hours, high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod or open mouth posture.
  • Clinical diagnosis; avoid throat examination or distress.
  • Secure airway in ICU or OR.
  • Then blood culture plus 3rd generation cephalosporin.
exam_pearl: Any option that delays securing the airway (workup, imaging, throat swab) is wrong as the immediate action in epiglottitis.

stem: Elderly presents to the Emergency Department with bright blood with his stool; he is known for colonic polyp and hypertension. On Ex he is pale and tachycardic. Vitals: BP 160/90, HR: 128. What is the most appropriate initial?
OptC: Oral iron ( yes I am sure)
why_right: An elderly man with bright red rectal bleeding who is pale and tachycardic (HR 128) has significant blood loss. The lead-in asks for the initial step, and in any GI bleed with haemodynamic compromise that is ABC resuscitation: large-bore IV access, IV fluids and blood transfusion, then localisation of the source. The BP of 160/90 does not reassure, because he is a known hypertensive and tachycardia is the earlier sign of shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urgent colonoscopy is the diagnostic and therapeutic test for lower GI bleeding (polyp is a likely source), but only after resuscitation and bowel preparation; it is never the first step in a tachycardic patient.
B. CT (angiography) is used to localise active bleeding in a patient who keeps bleeding, after resuscitation has started; it does not replace volume and blood replacement.
C. Oral iron treats chronic iron deficiency anaemia in a stable outpatient; it does nothing for acute haemorrhage with tachycardia.
key_concept:
Any GI bleed: resuscitate first, then find the source.
  • Step 1: assess haemodynamics (HR, BP, pallor, postural drop)
  • Unstable: two large-bore IV lines, crystalloid, crossmatch and transfuse, correct anticoagulation
  • Lower GI bleed once stable: colonoscopy after preparation
  • Ongoing brisk bleed: CT angiography, then embolisation
  • Massive bright red bleed with shock: exclude an upper GI source with endoscopy
exam_pearl: A normal or high BP in a known hypertensive with HR 128 is still shock; 'initial' means resuscitation.

stem: A patient with recent rectal surgery comes to you with absent pulses up to the femoral area. How will you manage such a case?
highlight_terms_source: absent pulses up to the femoral area
why_right: This recall is the garbled version of a known question: after rectal surgery a patient develops a thrombosis extending up to the femoral level (DVT from popliteal to common femoral vein). For a postoperative DVT without contraindication, first-line treatment is therapeutic low molecular weight heparin, enoxaparin, which is then continued or bridged to oral anticoagulation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Unfractionated heparin is preferred when LMWH is unsuitable: severe renal impairment, very high bleeding risk needing rapid reversal, or acute arterial limb ischaemia. None of these is stated.
C. IVC filter is reserved for proximal DVT/PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding) or for clot progression despite adequate anticoagulation.
D. Thrombolysis is contraindicated soon after major surgery and is kept for massive PE with shock or limb-threatening iliofemoral DVT, not routine DVT.
key_concept:
Postoperative VTE treatment ladder.
  • DVT or stable PE: LMWH (enoxaparin) first line
  • Renal failure: unfractionated heparin
  • Anticoagulation contraindicated: IVC filter
  • PE with shock: thrombolysis (recent surgery is a relative contraindication)
  • Acute arterial limb ischaemia: IV unfractionated heparin, then embolectomy or revascularisation
exam_pearl: If the stem truly means absent ARTERIAL pulses (cold, pale, painful limb), it is acute limb ischaemia and IV unfractionated heparin is the first step.

stem: A 17-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Department for polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and an unintentional weight loss over the past month. He has abdominal pain and drowsiness for the last 21 hours. His medical and family history are unremarkable. He is not on any medications. On physical examination, he looks sick with dry mucous membrane, tachypnea, and tachycardia with clear chest auscultation. Abdominal examination shows diffuse mild tenderness with normal bowel sounds. Intravenous 0.9% saline is initiated. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia 120/min. Chest radiograph is normal (see lab results). Blood pressure 95/53 mmHg. Heart rate 119/min. Respiratory rate 20/min. Temperature 37.2 C. Oxygen saturation 95%. BMI 19 kg/m2. Sodium 130 (134-146 mmol/L). Potassium 4.4 (3.5-5.1 mmol/L). Chloride 96 (97-108 mmol/L). Bicarbonate 10 (21-28 mmol/L). Blood urea nitrogen 15 (2.8-8.9 mmol/L). Creatinine 115 (44-115 umol/L). Random glucose 25 (3.9-5.5 mmol/L). ABG: HCO3 10 (22-28 mmol/L), pH 7.10 (7.36-7.45). RBC 5 (4.7-6.1 x10^12/L male; 4.2-5.4 female). Hb 130 (130-170 g/L male; 120-160 female). WBC 14 (4.5-10.5 x10^9/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
why_right: Glucose 25, pH 7.10 and bicarbonate 10 with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss in a 17-year-old is diabetic ketoacidosis from new-onset type 1 diabetes. Saline has "already been initiated" and potassium is 4.4 (not below 3.3), so the next step is IV insulin to stop ketogenesis and lower glucose, with potassium added to fluids as it falls.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV ceftriaxone: afebrile with a clear chest and normal radiograph; mild leukocytosis is common in DKA. Antibiotics are right only when an infective trigger is found.
C. IV potassium chloride: K 4.4 is normal; potassium is added to the fluids once insulin starts and K falls. Replacing potassium before insulin is needed only when K is below 3.3.
D. IV sodium bicarbonate: reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); pH 7.10 corrects with fluids and insulin.
key_concept:
DKA order: fluids, check K, insulin, then treat the trigger.
  • Diagnosis: hyperglycemia + metabolic acidosis + ketosis
  • Step 1: 0.9% saline resuscitation
  • K below 3.3: replace potassium before insulin
  • K 3.3 or above: start IV insulin infusion (low dose, 0.1 IU/kg/hr)
  • Bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9
  • Then find the precipitant (missed insulin, infection)
exam_pearl: If the stem had K below 3.3, potassium replacement would come before insulin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B (MG).

stem: A patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Laboratory results show: Blood glucose 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, Bicarbonate 15 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: The labs confirm DKA (glucose 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 15). The initial management is IV fluid resuscitation plus IV regular insulin infusion, after checking potassium is not low, because fluids correct the profound dehydration and fixed-rate IV insulin stops ketogenesis and closes the anion gap.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV bicarbonate is reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); at pH 7.15 it adds no benefit and risks hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis.
B. Subcutaneous insulin is used once DKA has resolved (overlapping with the infusion before stopping it); absorption is unreliable in a dehydrated acidotic patient, so it is not the initial treatment here.
key_concept:
DKA ladder: fluids, potassium, insulin, find the trigger.
  • Fluids first: 0.9% saline bolus, then 0.45% saline
  • Check K: if below 3.3, replace before insulin
  • Regular insulin IV infusion 0.1 U/kg/hr
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls, continue insulin until acidosis resolves
  • Bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9
  • Switch to SC basal insulin with overlap once resolved
exam_pearl: If the options separate fluids from insulin, fluids alone come first; if potassium is low, potassium comes before insulin.

Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0693).

stem: 10-year-old child presented to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and deep breathing. Laboratory results: Random blood glucose: 380 mg/dL; ABG: pH = 7.0, HCO3- = 10 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Glucose 380 mg/dL, "pH = 7.0", "HCO3- = 10", vomiting and deep breathing define severe DKA. The "most appropriate initial management" is IV fluid resuscitation followed by a continuous IV regular insulin infusion, which corrects dehydration, lowers glucose and stops ketogenesis.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV bicarbonate is not routine and in children is linked to cerebral edema and hypokalemia. It is considered only in extreme acidosis (pH below about 6.9) or life-threatening hyperkalemia.
C. Subcutaneous insulin with oral hydration suits only mild DKA in an alert child who tolerates fluids. With pH 7.0 and vomiting, absorption and oral intake are unreliable.
D. Raising bicarbonate does not stop ketosis; only insulin switches off ketone production. This option misunderstands the pathophysiology.
key_concept:
Severe DKA (pH <7.1 or HCO3 <5): IV fluids then IV insulin infusion.
  • Diagnosis: glucose ≥200 mg/dL, pH <7.3 or HCO3 <15 (ISPAD 2022: <18), ketones
  • Fluids first, then regular insulin 0.1 U/kg/h; confirm K is not low before insulin
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls; continue insulin until acidosis resolves
  • No routine bicarbonate
  • Main pediatric risk: cerebral edema
exam_pearl: Bicarbonate is the classic distractor in DKA: insulin, not alkali, clears ketoacidosis.

Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0246B).
