stem: A previously healthy 11-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of vomiting and diarrhea. His mother reports decreased oral intake and increasing lethargy over the past 12 hours. On examination, he is drowsy but arousable, and his breath has a fruity (nail polish-like) odor. Vital signs reveal mild hypotension. Laboratory results show: Random blood sugar (RBS): 8.9 mmol/L, Serum sodium: 131 mmol/L, Bicarbonate: 15 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of his current condition?
why_right: This recall's key is DKA because the child has vomiting, lethargy, hypotension (dehydration), a fruity (nail polish like) breath from acetone and a low bicarbonate of 15, the ketotic acidosis picture. Among the options DKA is the only diagnosis that accounts for ketones plus metabolic acidosis; the other options name a single lab finding or a non ketotic state.
why_wrong_block:
B. Uncontrolled hyperglycemia: describes a glucose number, not the cause of the acidosis and fruity breath; and RBS 8.9 mmol/L is not markedly high.
C. Hyponatremia: sodium 131 is a mild consequence of vomiting and diarrhea, not the cause of drowsiness and ketotic breath.
D. Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: needs very high glucose and high osmolality with little or no ketosis; here glucose is near normal and the breath is ketotic.
key_concept:
DKA needs hyperglycemia + acidosis + ketosis.
  • Clinical: vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, lethargy, fruity breath, Kussmaul breathing.
  • Labs (ISPAD 2022): pH < 7.3 or HCO3 < 18, ketonemia or ketonuria, glucose > 11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL).
  • HHS: very high glucose and osmolality, minimal ketones.
  • Ketosis with normal glucose after poor intake: starvation ketosis.
exam_pearl: Fruity breath means ketones; check the glucose before calling it DKA.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant listed under 2536 (Q: block).

stem: A 50-year-old man is complaining of pain affecting the wrist joints bilaterally, second and third proximal interphalangeal joints, and right knee joint for the last 4 months. His examination revealed active arthritis at both wrists and second and third proximal interphalangeal joints (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: wrist joints bilaterally, second and third proximal interphalangeal joints
why_right: Symmetric arthritis of both wrists and 2nd/3rd PIPs for 4 months with active arthritis on exam is new rheumatoid arthritis. This recall's key combines DMARD maintenance (methotrexate as the anchor, with hydroxychloroquine) and short-term prednisone as a bridge, because steroids control synovitis within days while DMARDs take weeks to months to work. The steroid is then tapered once the DMARDs take effect.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate: the correct anchor DMARD, but alone it gives no rapid control of active synovitis while it takes effect; in this recall the bridge is the missing piece.
B. Methotrexate and sulfasalazine: an acceptable DMARD combination, but it still lacks the steroid bridge for active arthritis.
C. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine: good maintenance DMARDs, but no bridging glucocorticoid for the currently active joints.
key_concept:
New active RA = DMARD (methotrexate based) for maintenance + short-term prednisone as a bridge.
  • Methotrexate is the cornerstone; hydroxychloroquine alone is not enough
  • Steroids act in days, DMARDs in weeks to months
  • Taper steroids once controlled; do not continue long term
  • Refractory or erosive disease: add a TNF inhibitor
  • Anti-CCP confirms RA; RA spares DIP joints
exam_pearl: When the stem says 'active arthritis' at diagnosis, choose the option that includes the steroid bridge.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: D (GB). Lab results referenced but not shown.

stem: 5 months old child admitted to hospital many times with pneumonia. Came now with cough and monophasic bilateral expiratory wheezing. What is the diagnosis test?
why_right: A 5 month old with recurrent pneumonia and a monophasic (single pitch, fixed) expiratory wheeze suggests a fixed central airway problem (tracheomalacia, airway compression such as a vascular ring, aspirated foreign body or congenital lesion) rather than asthma or bronchiolitis. The lead in is the diagnostic test, and flexible bronchoscopy directly visualizes the airway, shows dynamic collapse or obstruction, and allows lavage.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chest x ray: useful to confirm each pneumonia episode, but it cannot show dynamic airway collapse or the cause of a fixed central obstruction.
B. CBC and blood culture: assess infection or sepsis in an acute episode, but do not explain why pneumonia keeps recurring with a fixed wheeze.
C. Spirometry: the diagnostic test for asthma or COPD in older children and adults; it needs cooperation and is not feasible at 5 months.
key_concept:
Wheeze type points to the site.
  • Polyphonic, variable wheeze: small airway disease (asthma, bronchiolitis).
  • Monophasic, fixed wheeze: central or focal obstruction.
  • Recurrent pneumonia in infancy: think structural, aspiration, foreign body, immune.
  • Tracheomalacia diagnosis: bronchoscopy; laryngomalacia: laryngoscopy.
exam_pearl: Infant + recurrent pneumonia + monophasic wheeze means look inside the airway: bronchoscopy, not spirometry.
